speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the Minister of Transport. Has the attention of the minister been drawn to a situation existing in Stellarton, Nova Scotia, which indicates that the car repair shop at Stellarton has been closed down and that this in addition to the 500 miners already out of work is, according to Mayor Sobey of
Stellarton, causing an extremely serious unemployment situation. I would point out that in addition to the closing of the repair shop I am informed by the mayor by telegram that there is also further lay-off of personnel on the Canadian National Railways at Stellarton.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subtopic: STELLARTON, NOVA SCOTIA    CLOSING OF RAILWAY REPAIR SHOP
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, perhaps I may be allowed to take this question as notice, and inquire what the position is from the Canadian National Railways and report later. Will my hon. friend let me see the telegram?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: STELLARTON, NOVA SCOTIA    CLOSING OF RAILWAY REPAIR SHOP
speechtext: I should be happy to do so. In view of the stage of the session at which we are, may I suggest that when the minister obtains the information he might make a statement to us, in view of the fact that the general situation was under discussion yesterday and that the information with regard to this matter did not come to my attention until this morning.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subtopic: STELLARTON, NOVA SCOTIA    CLOSING OF RAILWAY REPAIR SHOP
speechtext: I will undertake to obtain the information as quickly as I can do so. I must point out to the hon. member, however, that the information I will get will be from the office of the Canadian National Railways at Montreal which, in turn, would have to get it from their maritime regional office. It may not be possible to get it in time before prorogation. However, I assure the hon. member that I will undertake to do it with all haste.

subtopic: STELLARTON, NOVA SCOTIA    CLOSING OF RAILWAY REPAIR SHOP
speechtext: We shall be here all day.

I have been coming to it all the time, Mr. Speaker, but I am right there now. This amendment does give civil servants a chance to opt out. Subsection 2 of the amended section 52 says that an election made under the section is irrevocable. To me there is almost a slight element of threat in that. In spite of what the minister said about his own preference, I do hope that the government, having approved this amendment, will not in any way hedge on it, because in my view what has happened, as I tried to say a moment ago, is that partial light has been let in on the minds of the government, and I hope that they will go further.
I just want to add this one thing. I have referred to the fact that in the deliberative assembly this matter was deliberated. It is surprising that the best the leader of the other place could say for this legislation was that it is not all bad. That was in the newspapers, Mr. Speaker, and I am able to tell you that it is accurate. I hope that in these circumstances, having made the change which has been made, having at last recognized the unanimous representations made by the representatives of the civil servants that this compulsory feature was obnoxious, the government will keep their minds open and, as I say, having gone a little way in the right direction, may find it in their hearts to go still further.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE PAYMENT OF DEATH BENEFITS UP TO MAXIMUM OF $5,000- CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENT

I have no sheets in either hand, Mr. Speaker, so perhaps I can keep in order. Something has been said this morning as to who should get the credit for the amendments that are now before us. Since the last speaker favours the amendments, he naturally talked in those terms, and since I do not like what is being done perhaps I should decide where to put the blame. I do not put the blame on the official opposition in this house or on Their Honours in the other place. I put the blame where it belongs, on the government, for accepting these amendments and moving their adoption as the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) has done this morning.
So far as the substance of the amendments is concerned, it is quite clear what is involved. As I understand it, the substance of these amendments is that arrangements will be made for those who are in government employ, on or before July 1-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE PAYMENT OF DEATH BENEFITS UP TO MAXIMUM OF $5,000- CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENT

The other provision set out in these amendments is for a coming into force clause. I understand that the reason for having a coming into force clause rather than the usual arrangement that the bill become law upon royal assent is, as the Minister of Finance said just now by way of interruption, so that the government can reconsider its position if it wishes to do so after November 1.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I believe that we have to pay some attention to what the government has announced as its intention, in the light of that coming into force clause which is proposed in these amendments. I understand it has been indicated that if a negligible number of persons, say of the order of 2 per cent, contract out, that will make no difference; but it has also been indicated that if as many as 25 per cent contract out, the government may decide not to proclaim the bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE PAYMENT OF DEATH BENEFITS UP TO MAXIMUM OF $5,000- CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENT

We are getting it clear. If there are 25 per cent who decide they do not want this provision, the bill will not be proclaimed. However, the understanding is that in between 2 per cent and 25 per cent the government will reconsider its position.
I must say that to me this is a strange form of democracy. What is being said is that if one person says no and three persons say yes, the bill will not be proclaimed. I would say that if the government wanted to amend the bill to modify the compulsory feature to make it possible for those who do not wish to have this insurance to deny themselves that right, the government might have done it in that way, with whatever modifications might be necessary. But to take this position that if one out of four does not want it the other three who do cannot have it-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE PAYMENT OF DEATH BENEFITS UP TO MAXIMUM OF $5,000- CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENT

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE PAYMENT OF DEATH BENEFITS UP TO MAXIMUM OF $5,000- CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENT

I realize that, and that is what I was saying. If the government wanted to modify the compulsory feature and make whatever change was necessary in the rates so as to have it on an optional basis, that in my view would have been a responsible way to approach this matter. But to put it on the basis of a veto, which is what is provided in this arrangement, is I think contrary to the democratic way of doing things. I put the blame where I believe it belongs. Perhaps the Minister of Finance did not think up this idea, and I will give him credit for moving his motion this morning reluctantly, but I point out it does not matter whether he moved it with reluctance or with exuberance, if the motion passes the result is the same.
I regret, Mr. Speaker, that the government has taken this position. As I say, I do not object to the government deciding to change the bill if it wishes to do so by making certain modifications on its own responsibility. But I think it is wrong, and I think it is unfair to have it announced to civil servants generally-it is almost a threat, if you like-that if 25 per cent, a decided minority, say no then the 75 per cent cannot have the advantages of this very beneficial piece of legislation. The government was very proud of this legislation. It was put to a vote several times by the government, and it was supported. The government insisted on knowing where the house stood on the matter.
I regret that the Minister of Finance has given in to this pressure, particularly in making the announcement that if 25 per cent are opposed to the legislation the other 75 per cent cannot have it. I do not think that is in keeping with true democracy.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE PAYMENT OF DEATH BENEFITS UP TO MAXIMUM OF $5,000- CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENT

I just want to add one word. This is a measure that is of benefit for civil servants, not for the government and not for the taxpayers of Canada. When it was represented in the other place, by this aggressive organization of maiden ladies here in Ottawa, that there should be a chance to opt out of the plan, the government felt that was perhaps not unreasonable. However, if more than 20 or 25 per cent do not want it, the plan just falls to the ground. It was devised on the assumption that all members of the civil service would be in it.
If you have an optional plan and a smaller group, then I think the arrangements should be made with an ordinary life insurance company to take out group insurance. This is another type of plan. I would have preferred the hon. member for Greenwood to

The discussion of the coal industry in this debate so far has proceeded on the basis of three assumptions. First, that the coal industry is indispensable to the economy of Canada, especially in times of national emergency. Second, that the satisfaction of the long run energy requirements of this country must depend in part on coal. The third assumption is that the coal industry, as a source of employment and earnings, is crucial to the industrial economy of Nova Scotia. These three considerations, Mr. Chairman, are of sufficient weight to provide a solid basis for a firm and generous policy of support to the coal industry. In the past this policy of encouragement has been carried forward in the main through, first, the small customs tariff, second, subventions on the movement of coal, and third, the Maritime Coal Production Assistance Act.
The customs tariff and especially the subventions policy had their origin in the competitive advantage and consequent threat of imported United States coal. Since 1928, approximately 31 million tons of Nova Scotia coal have been moved at an expenditure of approximately $40 million. As long as the chief threat to the Canadian coal industry came from imported United States coal, this subvention policy seemed adequate to maintain stability in the industry. However, within recent years the source and form of the competition to the coal industry has changed abruptly. The major form of present competition is not from imported coal but from fuel substitutes, and fuel substitutes in some cases of Canadian and not foreign origin.
The dominion coal board report states:
It appeared certain that this factor, namely, the inroads of oil and natural gas would occasion further dislocation in the industry as pipeline facilities expanded and the railroads pressed forward their program of dieselization and conversion.
Later the report states:
The Niagara power development and the St. Lawrence seaway and power project threaten to make available a supply of secondary power which would involve the temporary displacement of some tonnages of coal as far east as Montreal.
I believe the new forms of competition have brought greater and more formidable
25, 1954	6707
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys difficulties in the development of a suitable coal policy. The difficulties are apparent because fuel substitutes are produced in Canada by fellow Canadians.
However formidable the difficulties, the only satisfactory attitude to the current crisis is an attitude of realism taking into account that the chief ingredient in the development of the coal industry is a product that will hold the market against fuel substitutes.
This view is accepted without question. It was recognized in the enactment of the Maritime Coal Production Assistance Act under whose terms millions have already been made available to the Dominion Steel and Coal Corporation and other coal companies for mechanization with the anticipation of lowering the cost of production. Up to the present time no lower costs have resulted from mechanization.
The president of Dosco now expresses doubt as to whether the deterioration in the market for coal will warrant the continuation of a mechanization program. But it should be borne in mind that an improved market outlook depends upon lowering production costs, and that each of these desirable outcomes is indispensable to the future of the coal industry. For that reason, Mr. Chairman, any reluctance to pursue the mechanization program, as a lower cost device, either on the part of the government or of the industry, must be resisted because such a position means that the industry expects a guaranteed market as a precondition of cost-reducing innovations, which are in themselves the only way to assure a coal market.
The program recently initiated by the provincial government, in co-operation with the industry, to stimulate the home consumption of coal is a step in the right direction. Sales in the home market have already decreased by 500,000 tons per year. Annual production of this magnitude creates employment for
1,000	men. Part of this decrease is due to the switchover by industry and domestic users from coal to oil. This program of stimulating consumption of coal in the maritime market deserves all possible encouragement, and I think it is important because it may hold the line against further encroachment of oil until the pay-off point is reached in certain research projects into new uses for coal.
Reference has already been made to the research being conducted at McGill University by Professor Mordell into the coal-fired gas turbine, in the fuel division of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys.
Though the coal crisis hit the headlines very dramatically this winter, scientists have

Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys been working quietly and painstakingly to discover ways by which coal may compete effectively with oil as a fuel and as an industrial raw material. Of particular interest and importance is the work of the Nova Scotia research foundation, not only because of its own research, but because it is in contact with research into coal being undertaken in Europe and the United States.
Among experiments which are outlined in the annual report of the Nova Scotia research foundation are, first, research into the burning of coal underground to recover energy and by-products. Underground gasification of coal would permit the use of thin seams of coal. Second, research into development of methods of handling and burning Nova Scotia coal to eliminate the nuisance of smoke, hand-firing and ash removal from domestic furnaces. Third, study into methods of coal carbonization. Interest in this process springs from the collection of coal tar chemicals as potential raw material in chemical industries.
I believe this research deserves all possible encouragement and public support.
Of all the research that is now going on into further uses of coal, no series of experiments is fraught with greater possibilities than the work now under way at Morgantown, West Virginia. Equipment developed by the United States bureau of mines, in association with the engineering firm of Babcock and Wilcox, is producing gas from coal in surface units.
If this gasification should prove to be suitable and economical for Nova Scotia coals, then the future markets for the industry may not be solid coal transported by subvention assistance to the central market, but a coal market at the pithead at conversion units turning coal into gas for domestic and industrial use in the maritimes and Quebec. Nova Scotia coals have been tested at Morgantown, and at some future date it is even possible that gas from Nova Scotia coal will move by pipe line into the large consuming centres.
If this type of research proves practical, then it may provide the real answer to the problem of a Nova Scotia coal industry.
I now come back to an earlier point, Mr. Chairman. All progress in the coal industry rests, in my judgment, on a more competitive fuel. It is commonly believed that the chief way of reducing costs is through mechanization. Up to the present time, no reduction in costs has occurred through the installation of big machinery. I am not advocating that this program should be stopped.


It is my belief however, given the proper motivation and the proper conditions, the human resources-the people in the industry -could increase productivity far beyond the expectations now placed on the installation of big machines. I believe this increased productivity could take place with greater rewards in form of income and human satisfaction. Maybe the chief error of modern business is to plan for every conceivable phase of the productive process except the proper motivation and satisfaction of the human resources.
I am glad the hon. member for Cape Breton South referred last night to the engineering know-how latent in the working force in the Cape Breton mines. That the human resources of the coal industry-and of most other industries-have untapped sources of ingenuity, skill and ideas is the first attitude to be taken towards this problem. How can one release this productivity? First, by setting up a structure within the mines whereby the combined creativeness of the work force can influence productive decisions. Second, by the development of a productivity yardstick that measures increased group performance and a reward system that puts punch into team work. Finally, by the acceptance by management and the union of each other as essential institutions in the industry.
I believe there exists today in the Nova Scotia coal industry a basis for the introduction of such a joint system of union-management co-operation. I am not advocating a speed-up. I am not advocating anything that will weaken either management or union. I am advocating a formula that will strengthen both as well as strengthen the industry.
The chief exponent of this type of relationship is a former union president and former research director of the United Steel Workers of America. At present he is on the staff of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. I refer to Mr. Joe Scanlon. Joe Scanlon has applied his productivity plans, based on the above ingredients, in a variety of industries with remarkable success. Unions like his approach to productivity and so do managements.
Last week I had the opportunity to discuss once again with Mr. Scanlon in Boston the success of his work in the German coal mines at the end of the war when coal production was one of the chief problems of Germany. Joe Scanlon's staff succeeded in achieving concrete results in improving the productivity of those mines. I believe the

same approach is worthy of serious consideration in connection with the Nova Scotia industry, because this industry is vital to the welfare of my province.
Mr. Chairman, discussion of the coal industry in Nova Scotia has centred in the main on the problems of the chief operator and the communities to which its operations extend. It is in that general vein that I have made my remarks up to the present time. However exclusive attention to the interests of the chief operator is not consistent with the welfare of other smaller communities.
When I return to my constituency I shall visit two communities now languishing because of the state of the coal industry, namely Inverness and Port Hood. When I return to Inverness, almost every miner in that community will be walking the main street because there is no market in which it is possible to dispose of their coal which is excellent for domestic purposes. Inverness town has been the chief casualty of the Nova Scotia coal industry, and already it has borne too great a share of the burden and sacrifices involved in the current adjustments of that industry.
I invite from the dominion coal board increased attention to the problems of the independent operators in the small communities, in finding markets and also in developing methods to share in a fair manner among all communities the burden of the present difficulties of the coal industry.

They face, of course, the problem which the hon. member for Inverness-Rich-mond just mentioned. Their problems are somewhat different from and possibly more difficult of solution than those of the larger operators. But in any event the problems of the future are much the same for all coal communities. The same or much the same solutions must be found if the coal industry is to survive in Nova Scotia. The implications, of course, reach far beyond the immediate areas I have named; for if the industry perishes, then the whole economy of the province, which is based to a substantial degree upon coal, will receive another of those shattering blows which it has received so often since confederation.
Since the last decades of the nineteenth century the coal industry has maintained a place of major importance in the economic life of Cumberland county. It has had varying fortunes, but to date it has always been able to survive all the dangers which have from time to time threatened it, although never before so ominously as at the present time.
To go back to the beginnings with us, history records that even in the distant days of the French settlements boatloads of coal from the Joggins seams went up and down the coast to fire the forges of the sturdy blacksmiths of the Acadian villages. That thought takes us back to the romantic days of Evangeline. I do not think Longfellow's poem mentions it, but I daresay that Basil the blacksmith was using Joggins coal. However, we are not living in the past, and certainly there is very little room to find any poetry in the coal situation as it exists today. Many descendants of those early Acadians, I may add, still find work in the pits of the Joggins area and they face now possibly another expulsion, an economic expulsion from their ancestral soil.
The problems of the Nova Scotia coal industry have, I know, been dealt with in considerable detail, and I think they are fairly well known to most members of the
6710	HOUSE OF
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys house, even to those who have no immediate concern with them. Lack of industrial development in the maritimes, distance from the markets of central Canada coupled with the nearness of American sources of supply, adverse natural conditions which are a very strong factor in the situation in Nova Scotia -the depth of the Springhill mines, for example-militating against low costs of production, the increasing use of hydroelectric power and finally, of course, the increasing competition from oil and natural gas, now undoubtedly in a stage of rapid intensification, these and the marketing difficulties which they create are the present emergent problems of the industry.
It has been said that our coal industry has itself to blame for very much of its present plight. I would be ready to allow a certain measure of truth to this, at least with regard to the past, but I think it is also true to say today, from what I have seen of management and labour relations, that both management and labour today realize fully the gravity of the situation and are ready and willing to play their part in the fight to save the industry. I know that both are giving very strong support to the campaign which has been inaugurated in the maritimes to promote the use of coal in preference to other fuels, chiefly oil. It is hoped that the campaign will win back a substantial market for coal. I believe that both management and labour are now willing to co-operate fully in the endeavour to attain a maximum in efficiency of production, something which is of vital importance to the Nova Scotia industry. Some progress of course has been made along this line, but it is a long and difficult road which they must travel. Certainly time will be needed before any substantial results can be obtained, and unfortunately the next few years will be crucial ones for the industry.
It has been generally forecast-indeed, I think it is the considered opinion of the dominion coal board-that by the middle sixties the increase in population and in industrial development in Canada will create a situation whereby the demand for coal will have reached a point at which the industry can maintain itself on at least its present level. Assuming the correctness of this forecast, the industry is not moribund in the sense that we must visualize a perpetually expanding program of governmental assistance to keep it on its feet. But, as I say, the next decade will be the crucial years, and undoubtedly the need for assistance to the coal mining industry will remain very great. Anyone questioning the wisdom of furnishing such assistance as may be required must, I think, weigh against the undoubtedly high
[Mr. Lusby.l

cost attendant upon that what I call the much higher cost, both tangible and intangible, of allowing the industry to perish.
At this stage all my remarks are made with the full and, I may say, the uneasy knowledge that as far as any prophecies for the future are concerned the whole picture may be completely changed by the coming of atomic power for industry. If it comes, as it undoubtedly will, it will probably affect profoundly the whole economic face of the country and, I hope, with benefit to the maritimes. But I think such speculation as that at the present time may be left, in the discussion of this subject, until such time as these possibilities of atomic power, strong though they undoubtedly are, have reached the stage of reality and the effect of atomic power upon the use of conventional fuel can be more accurately determined.
On the basis of confirmed knowledge the death of our coal industry would in time of peace, in my opinion, create a very serious sapping of our economic strength and our industrial prospects. It would mean that the maritime provinces would be pushed deeper into the economic mire. It would mean widespread unemployment, distressed areas, the depopulation of towns and villages, for one of the tragedies of the situation is that in most cases the coal mining community is almost entirely dependent upon that one industry. It would mean that the people from these towns and villages would have to undergo a forced exile to distant parts of the country, or perhaps even beyond their own borders. A situation like that would undoubtedly provide a spawning ground for communism and its evil doctrines.
In time of war-I know this has been touched on before but I think perhaps it is not amiss that I should mention it again- the loss of the industry would be revealed as a very serious gap in our national security, a serious impairment to our capacity for either defence or attack. For the proof of that statement I think we have to go no farther than to the days of the last world conflict. Coal and steel were the twin pillars of our war effort then, and so far no adequate proved substitute for either is at hand, while the threat of aggression hangs over us almost constantly. I need hardly emphasize that this is no time for any gambling with matters which may affect our national security.
When we consider therefore the costs, the penalties attendant upon the loss of the Canadian coal industry, I think we can assert with confidence, as I do, that it is a matter of national self-interest that this government, in conjunction of course with the provincial

governments immediately concerned, should bend every effort to ensure that such a loss shall not occur.
The principle of federal assistance to the coal industry is not a novel one. We have the system of freight subventions instituted in 1928, over a quarter of a century ago, which throughout that time has been a mainstay of the industry. We have such acts as the Maritime Coal Production Assistance Act under which loans are available for mechanization and modernization of mines. In Nova Scotia that has not produced great results yet, but there are possibilities and some work has been done. I am very glad to know that the government, as the estimates under discussion show, realizes fully the desirability of continuing and expanding the system of freight subventions.
There is also the assistance given in connection with the use of coal in the manufacture of iron and steel. We have the dominion coal board itself which I think has done a great deal to aid the industry. However, I think within the limits of its existing statutory powers it could be made an even more efficient instrument to that end. The government has furnished substantial assistance in connection with the very promising development at McGill University of a coal-fired gas turbine engine. That may prove to be of some substantial help to the coal industry once it is brought to perfection.
All these measures have accomplished much to aid the coal industry in its fight for survival, and I say without any hesitation that all the expenditures involved may be considered money very well spent in the national interest. In another aspect there has been a promising beginning. I refer to the inquiry now under way into the possibilities of producing more electricity from coal in the maritimes. I am rather particularly interested in that because one of the earliest, if not the earliest, of the successful developments on the North American continent in producing electricity from coal at or near the pithead was carried out at Chig-necto in my constituency.
As a matter of fact most of the electricity used in the county of Cumberland today is produced by a coal-fired plant situated at Maccan near the River Hebert-Joggins mines. There is, however, one field of assistance to the coal mining industry which I consider is very largely unexplored in this country. That is the field of research to discover new and commercially practicable uses for coal apart altogether from its conventional use as fuel. That, incidentally, is a field which would not be affected by any development of atomic power.
6711
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys
It has long been known, of course, that coal is a potential source of numerous products of high market value. I have a list here of a few examples which are as follows: perfume, gasoline, alcohol, disinfectant, dyes, ammonia, and fertilizer. Since the list ranges from perfume to fertilizers, one can see how wide a range of potential products coal contains. In essence, all of these products are in the blackness of a lump of coal. In most cases they are extractable by scientific methods already known, but unfortunately not yet at competitive costs. Much has been done abroad in the way of discovering new and better methods of extraction. The last speaker mentioned some experiments being conducted in the United States. The Nova Scotia government, within the limits of its resources, is doing its utmost to aid the coal industry by maintaining a close liaison with the experiments that are being conducted by the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. It is keeping in touch also with European experiments which have as their objective the development of soil conditioners from coal.
I understand that some Nova Scotia coal has been successfully used as the basis of an experiment along that line. It seems to me the federal government has not yet concerned itself to the extent it should in this field. I should like to suggest that no matter what is being done abroad we should not be content to await results from the United States or from Europe. I feel that Canada should be m the forefront of this, as in all other fields of industrial research.
One of the statutory objectives of the dominion coal board is, I believe, as follows:
The board may undertake or cause to be under-ta / ^fsearches and investigations with respect to:
(c) The physical and chemical characteristics of coal produced in Canada with a view to developing new uses therefor.
I should like to urge that the existing powers of the board in that respect be put to much wider use than has been the case so far. This will involve a substantial expenditure undoubtedly, but I am firmly convinced that, in common with all sums which have been already expended and are being expended to assist the coal industry, these further sums devoted to that purpose could be considered money very well spent in the national interest.
Finally, Mr. Chairman, I should like to assure the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys that we in Cumberland county, and I know the same holds true for the rest of Nova Scotia as well as for other coal producing areas in Canada, appreciate greatly the time and attention that he has given to the problems of the coal industry in Canada. The

I have two desires in rising, Mr. Chairman, first of all, to get what I have to say said quickly, and secondly to say the things that need to be said. I wish, at the outset, to commend the minister for the manner in which he has attacked the problem. I believe his introductory speech last night was a model and I should like to encourage him to continue the deep interest he has already shown.
I want to say something to him in all kindness, and I hope he will not be offended, but I believe it is a matter he needs to have drawn to his attention. At the moment, we in Alberta have the idea that he gives altogether too much attention to his quarrel with the Social Credit movement in that province. If he would just forget his quarrel with that government and with that movement, and remember that he is the responsible minister of the crown for this whole country, then he would not say things like those to which the hon. member for Macleod referred last night, wondering what Alberta is doing about this coal problem. I thought I really should say that in all kindness because the minister has great possibilities, and I want to see him attain them with all the speed of which he is capable.
In respect of the problem of coal which confronts us, I do not wish to review the various aspects of the problem. I know they are very difficult. I believe I know pretty well all the things that stand in the way of finding a solution for Alberta's coal problem. When I first came to Ottawa I devoted a great deal of attention to the subject of coal, and did what a member could to help get our coal down into Ontario and Quebec markets. In those days we had not discovered the gas and oil in Alberta to any such extent as we have since discovered it. We had not conceived the feasibility of the idea of bringing that gas and oil down here by pipes. Now, of course, those things are practically an accomplishment. I gave up talking about coal for a while because I realized that there seemed to be difficulties which were insuperable, but my interest has continued nevertheless.
There are three or four things I think that need to be pointed out as a sort of summary to what has already been said. What seems to be worrying the coal producing areas more than anything else at the moment is the unemployment that has resulted in the coal producing communities. If we could somehow manage to provide employment for the men who have been displaced by a reduction in markets for coal, and the final closing of
[Mr. Lusby.I

the mines, then the urgency of the problem at the moment would, in large measure, be eliminated. I am sure the minister realizes that. What is troubling the people, for example, in the Shaughnessy area is that they do not know where to turn to find work with which to support their families. I mention Shaughnessy, but that is only one of the mines that have been seriously affected in my constituency.
There is one aspect of the question that the hon. member for Cape Breton South mentioned last night which I must say has given me a somewhat new slant. I gather from a statement of the minister to which the hon. member referred, that the minister foresees a time in the not too distant future when we, in Canada, may have a need for all the fuel production of which we are capable. I do not know whether I am misinterpreting the report or whether the reporter misinterpreted the minister, but I do not really quite see how there could be such a development of Canadian industry and population within 11 years as to make the country capable of using all the fuel productive capacity we have. If there is, so much the better.
I believe another matter the hon. member for Cape Breton South mentioned last night is most pertinent to the needs of the situation connected with the problem. We must take steps to see that no mine shall have its coal producing capacity destroyed or seriously impaired through disuse over a number of years. I believe that is a very important point. In trying to draft a policy for the next two years, we ought to bear that in mind. I am sure the minister has done so.
The next matter, to which of course everyone referred, is the developing competition with coal on the part of other fuels, such as oil, gas, gasoline, electricity and finally atomic power. There is a probability that even solar energy will be competitive. Men are talking about a means of taking energy out of the sun and using it for industrial and domestic purposes. We must recognize that competition is an actual fact, and will continue to be a fact. In so far as western Canada and eastern Canada are concerned, the competition of United States coal with our own fuel is and is likely long to be a serious matter for us. In that connection I am not sure that I have the figures correct, but the minister will check me if I am wrong. However, as I recall it we are importing from the United States something like two tons of coal for every ton we are producing in Canada. Is that correct?

I wish now to say a word in respect of Alberta's coal producing capacity, as a whole. Alberta is peculiar in several respects as regards her coal production. She produces a wide variety of coal. Some of it is almost as valuable as anthracite, and then we produce coal all the way down the scale, until we come to something that is very close to lignite. That is a point worth bearing in mind.
Then the next point to bear in mind is that Alberta's mines are rather widely distributed, although it is a fact that they are all in the one province of Alberta.

I thank the minister for that information. It makes the disparity less aggravating. And yet, even those figures are impressive, are they not?
Then, I was about to refer to the distribution of Alberta mines, which means that if we use the different kinds of coal coming from the different mines in Alberta, in the development of industry for the future, we have a wide possibility of variation in industrial development in Alberta. That is another point worth mentioning.
The next important fact about Alberta coal is that, in a general way, it is economical to produce. We do not have anything to compare with the difficulties confronting the people of Nova Scotia, who have to go down under the sea floor in order to find the coal and bring it out. On the other hand, in Alberta we have a good many areas where strip mining is quite practicable, and indeed was practised during the second world war. That also is a point which should not be forgotten particularly when making a plea for Alberta's coal production.

The next important thing in respect of Alberta is that she is capable of tremendous industrial development. Up to the present time of course the industrial centres in Canada have been in Ontario and Quebec, and no doubt a good many people in those provinces would like to have it continue so. But I believe when they begin to think in terms of the nation, and of over-all security, they will realize it will be greatly to their advantage to have a vast amount of industrial development take place in Alberta, Saskatchewan and British Columbia so that there will be two powerful industrial areas in Canada. That ought to be borne in mind when we plan.
One could give a good example from the last war, to illustrate the point I have in mind. I would refer to the fact that while I was in Great Britain in 1941 as a member of the Empire Parliamentary Association delegation from Canada, I was told that Great Britain at the time of the war was divided into 12 areas. The aim was to make each of those 12 areas self-sufficient so that if an enemy were to conquer even 11 of them, the twelfth could still carry on and support a substantial war effort, with the hope ultimately of expelling the foe and defeating him.
I suggest that is a good thing for us to reflect upon in Canada. If a foe were to come to our country and destroy the industry of Ontario and Quebec, in large measure it would leave Canada almost defenceless from an industrial point of view. I think that is not a sound condition to encourage for the future, when there is so much danger. What I say strengthens my general contention that we should keep in mind the possibility of making Alberta the great industrial centre in Canada which it is capable of becoming.
Therefore it is of great importance that we preserve the coal mines in Alberta, and maintain their coal producing capacity. That is a matter which I suggest is very much worth remembering. To have a powerful industry developed in Alberta would strengthen us in both peace and war. In peacetime it would enable us to support a much larger population, and in wartime of course it would give us additional fighting strengtn.
What is the solution? There is the great problem. I do not hesitate to say right now that I think the solution is increased subventions to put Alberta coal into Ontario and Quebec so as to displace American coal. I know about the objections to shutting out American coal. That subject has been referred to by previous speakers. But everybody knows-and I wish to be careful not to use
6714	HOUSE OF
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys the wrong word-about the unpredictability of the labour unions in the United States. It would be possible for those labour unions in the United States to create a disturbance while we were in a war which might shut us off from our supply of coal from the United States, and thus embarrass us most seriously in our endeavour to keep up industrial production in Ontario and Quebec. We might as well face that fact now, while we can do something about it.
Consequently, from a national standpoint I think it is of compelling importance that we produce our own coal and get it into these two industrial provinces even as a temporary measure where it will be sorely needed. If we do not later feel that we can stand economically the financial strain of providing continually those subventions for both Alberta and Nova Scotia, then, as was suggested last night by the hon. member for Macleod, we might endeavour to determine by such study as is possible just about how many of these coal mines we need to close ultimately, and then determine the policy of closing these coal mines one by one, two by two or three by three, as the case may be, after warning those engaged in the coal mines concerned that their work will discontinue at a certain time. Then we would have to make provision for their reabsorption into the economy of Canada.
I think that would be a sound method of approach, and I commend it to the minister. It may be that over a long period it will not be found economically feasible to support the coal producing capacity of Canada. If so, then at least let us go about the problem in a sensible way, and endeavour to have a plan of procedure whereby the closing of our mines would inflict the least possible damage on the Canadian economy.
It has been pointed out that the processing of the coal probably offers the way out. I realize that Germany has had wonderful success in this kind of development, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond. It is true that Germany has had phenomenal success in processing coal. But let us remember that Germany has 66 million people, and that they are rather closely concentrated. The result is that when products are processed from coal there is a ready market for them. Contrast that condition of population with our own. We have 15 million people thinly spread out over some 3,500 miles of territory. If a person were to establish a coal processing plant which would produce fur coats, which I understand the Germans produce, or any of the three or four dozen of the products which they have found it to be greatly to their advantage


to produce, we would be handicapped seriously by the shortage of markets locally and even from a national standpoint. The cost of transporting the finished products from Ontario to Alberta or from Alberta to Ontario or from Alberta to the Yukon would be almost prohibitive. Having that in mind, I think we shall stop looking to the processing of coal as an immediate source of remedy for the problem which confronts us, no matter how much possibility there may be in the processing of coal some time in the future-I am altogether in favour of processing, I may say.
I believe I have said about all I had in mind to say. I will repeat once more, I do believe that it would be altogether in the interest of Canada to give notice to the United States just as soon as we can, and as kindly as we can, that we do not feel that it is in the interests of the United States or of Canada that Canada should be largely dependent upon her friendly neighbour for coal or for any other fuel. After all, we intend to be a great nation. It is vitally in the interest of the United States that we should be a great nation. If calamity should befall her she would have someone on whom to rely for assistance. If we were too greatly integrated with the United States and calamity befell her it would involve us also. I do believe that if we approach the United States people in that attitude they will soon come to agree with our thinking that we should immediately proceed to import our coal needs from Alberta and from the maritimes to Quebec and Ontario. If we grant the subventions which are necessary to bring these coals into these two provinces I think probably that will prove to be the best immediate method of attacking the problem.

I have listened with a great deal of interest to the thought-provoking speeches which have been made on this coal problem from the various quarters of the house. The story of the situation that the coal industry finds itself in has been pretty well told. I could supplement that story to some extent by the story of the situation of the coal mining industry of Vancouver island, which happens to be our oldest industry there, apart from the original furtrading period; but I believe it would be repetitious if I were to do that at this stage. I will merely say that the facts of the industry there are similar to those which other hon. members have described in other parts of the country.
In view of the kind of speeches that have been made upon this subject, which shows that some hon. members have been giving

this problem a great deal of serious attention, I found myself rather disturbed last night by the reaction that the minister appeared to have to the speech which was made by the hon. member for Cape Breton South. Apparently his only reaction to the serious proposal which the hon. member put forward for the development of a national fuel policy under a national fuel board was some rather flippant interjection about nationalization. I should like to suggest that if the minister is going to allow his prejudices about "izations" and "isms" or anything of that kind to stand in the way of his taking a constructive and thoughtful approach to the solution of this problem, that is not the serious attitude which should properly be taken by a minister of the crown in this country. Before this discussion is over I hope the minister will make clear that he has a more serious interest in his duties than was indicated by the remark he made in reference to the speech by the hon. member for Cape Breton South. At the time the remark was interjected I happened to be glancing at a report I received in my mail box, the annual report of the Canadian Commercial Corporation, which I notice is a company apparently owned by the government of Canada, and which has been entrusted with finances to the extent of something over $196 million.
When a minister of a government which has been responsible for bringing into being an organization of this kind takes a flippant attitude towards suggestions made in all seriousness that we should try to take an over-all look at the question of fuel in this country, then I suggest it is not in keeping with the realities of life in Canada as we have them today. I myself have suggested, for example, that we should try to seek a more co-ordinated approach to the transportation problem in this country. Certainly no two things are more important and basic in the industrial era than transportation and fuel. Therefore I wish to emphasize the importance of the suggestion being made by the hon. member for Cape Breton South that this is not something which can be considered apart from other aspects of our Canadian economy; and if the minister is content to allow to continue what I would call a state of economic balkanization in the country, it will only lead to further and further troubles. Surely, in this day and age he should agree that this is something which should be approached from the over-all picture, and that we should seek in this parliament to guide and direct a policy which will be in the interests of all the people of

speechtext: There is a statutory vote for the coal board of $400,000. It is an old thing. I should like to call the minister's attention to the fact that there is a tariff of 50 cents a ton on bituminous coal at the United States border, but there is a drawback on that tariff of 49 cents permitted on imported coal when it is used for metallurgical purposes. We in turn have the $400,000 as some concession to the Canadian industry that uses coal for the making of steel. I would suggest that the coal board take a look at that. We are spending $400,000 on our own industry, which wipes out the effect of the tariff of 50 cents a ton. When you grant a drawback of 49 cents a ton to the importer you wipe out the effect of the tariff. If that tariff was to protect the Canadian bituminous industry in the first place, then it should remain and have that effect. To put it on and then wipe it out, because most of the coal imported is used for industrial purposes, does not seem to make sense. I am not objecting to the vote here. I think our industry is entitled to that amount of money, if we continue to grant the drawback to importers of the United States coal who use it for metallurgical purposes. I am bringing that to the attention of the coal board and the minister and I would urge them to take a look at this old statutory provision and see whether it is not having some effect in encouraging the importation of United States coal.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have listened with interest to the comments of the hon. member for Cape Breton South not only today but in his speech last night during which he emphasized that we should give encouragement to the building and strengthening of our steel industry. I believe that that statutory provision was designed in the first place to encourage our steel industry. The steel industry of Nova Scotia does not use United States coal and therefore it is given the equivalent of the tariff conditions other companies enjoy.
I wish to thank hon. members for the constructive speeches they have made concerning the problems of the coal industry. I was somewhat surprised at the very mild tone of the speech by the hon. member for Lethbridge this morning. He referred to a private quarrel I had with the Social Credit party. I do not mind admitting that I do not subscribe to their theories, but in so far as the coal industry is concerned I have no quarrel with them. I would like to refer to

Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys some of the remarks made in this debate, with particular reference to the remarks made by the hon. member for Macleod last evening.
He referred to a question he had asked in this house some time ago and to the answer I gave at that time. He gave no notice of that question; it was directed to the Minister of Labour; and in turn it was referred to me without notice. He said my reply was a cheap political answer. He is entitled to his opinion. But I am going to say that I think his question had some political implications. However, I am very pleased with the result that seemed to stem from that question and answer. The following week the Alberta government announced they were providing $100,000 for the rehabilitation of miners, and I hope that that question and answer had some influence on their decision.
Several hon. members have asked for a national fuel policy. This is an old story. Ever since I have been in parliament that proposal has always been brought up on these estimates. But as yet I have never met anyone who could state concisely what he meant by a "national fuel policy" or "national coal policy".
This government's policy in regard to coal has been clearly stated. For the past 26 years it has been the policy of this and other federal governments to assist Canadian coal to market by means of freight subventions. Those subventions are designed to make Canadian coal competitive with the United States imported coal. By the approval of the estimates now before this house this policy will be extended for the year 1954.
Assistance to the industry has also been given in other ways, as outlined in my statement to the committee, by research, by way of loans for mechanization, and assistance to the mine operators by way of studies of preparation and mining problems. Several hon. members have rightly stressed the importance of research. In my statement I outlined some of the research projects in which this government is engaged at the present time. We have one of our fuel division engineers in Europe studying and observing the experiments being carried on over there.
Just a few days ago the report of the British fuel commission was issued and it mentioned a new process being used in France, and I think also in Holland, to convert bituminous coal to anthracite. The chief of the fuels division in the last couple of days sent word to our man in England to be sure to look at this experiment before he returns.
[Mr. Prudham.l
Other forms of energy and fuel do not come under the jurisdiction of the dominion coal board, but just for a moment I would like to refer to these other fields of fuel and energy to show how they fit into the national picture. Up until a very few months ago this government had no stated policy in regard to natural gas for the simple reason that we had no gas with which to deal. Until the government of Alberta declared a surplus of gas for export this government had no jurisdiction. I need not take up the time of the committee to review recent developments in this field, because they have already been debated and carefully examined during the present session. To put it briefly, I might state that the government's policy was outlined by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, as recorded at page 2929 of Hansard of March 13, 1953, and I quote his words:
Therefore the policy of the government of Canada is to refuse permits for moving natural gas by pipeline across an international boundary until such time as we are convinced that there can be no economic use, present or future, for that natural gas within Canada.
The government's gas policy has not changed since that statement, and I am sure hon. members are very pleased to note the progress that has been made toward the construction of the east-west gas pipe line.
Since 1907 the federal government has rigidly controlled the export of electricity from Canada. During the last war the government initiated a project which is known as the Chalk River project for the development of atomic energy. We are all very pleased to know that Canada is in the forefront of progress in this field. Canada's atomic research is directed to peacetime application.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce announced to the house just recently that the method of development of electric power from this source is now well advanced. The hydroelectric power sources in Ontario will soon have been fully exploited, and other sources such as natural gas, atomic energy, as well as coal and oil, will, of necessity, have to be used to supplement the hydro power.
In a country developing as rapidly as Canada, we cannot have a static or rigid policy. Any federal government policy in regard to resource development must, of necessity, be flexible and capable of meeting the challenge of changing conditions.
It is all very well for Premier Manning and the Social Credit members from Alberta to try to "pass the buck" to this government by making the vague statement that we should have a national fuel policy. I say that because I have here a press clipping which

quotes Premier Manning as stating, when he announced his $100,000 fund, that the only-cure for this problem was a national fuel policy.
In 1930 the resources of the western provinces were transferred from this government to the provincial governments and with that transfer the provincial governments assumed the responsibility for the development as well as the benefit they would derive from these resources. Since 1935 the Alberta government has received in coal fees, rentals, and royalties, more than $8 million. During the same period the federal government has paid out $16,300,000 by way of freight subventions. This last figure does not include special wartime payments and production subsidies amounting to over $5,800,000. The estimates now before us provide more than $2,500,000 additional for the same purpose this year. The coal industry is suffering because of the development of gas and oil. I do not think it seems reasonable for the provincial government of Alberta to try to sidestep its responsibility with regard to coal simply by calling for a national fuel policy.

6718	HOUSE OF
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys has already taken place concerning this matter. I listened attentively last night and today to speeches made about the coal problem. I must say that I was impressed with the seriousness and the earnestness with which this problem has been discussed.
I particularly want to mention the speech delivered today by the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond. I thought his contribution to the debate was excellent and down to earth. He evidently has given a great deal of thought to this problem with which his own province is faced, and which is perhaps one of the great problems of the mari-times. I believe that the more we study what he had to say the more we will see in it by way of possible improvement in the coal situation.
I must say of course that the problem in western Canada is considerably different from the problem in the east, if for no other reason than the fact that we have been developing for some years now our oil and gas resources, and the outstanding development that has taken place has contributed in no small measure to the difficulties under which the coal mining industry carries on. We have in Alberta cheap natural gas and oil, both of which compete, in fact in many places more than compete, with coal. So there is little wonder that we have difficulty there.
It is quite true to say that the development of oil and gas in such quantities has contributed to the real problems faced by the coal people. In addition, we of course have great quantities of propane being used now far and wide by the farmers and other rural dwellers, so there is no wonder that there is difficulty. However, there are some spots which I think should begin to show a little light at the other end of the tunnel. I do not know how far we can look for relief for the coal industry to the experiments and research that are being carried out to try to find successful conversion methods. However, the other day I was talking with a man who seems to know something about conversion and he tells me that there is a good possibility that certain coals in the foothills of the Rocky mountains not too far from the city of Calgary could be converted successfully into electric power at the mine head.
The mining of the coal is quite cheap. The conducting lines for the electricity would be short enough to make possible the taking of the power to the northwestern United States and the selling of it there to the northwest power pool at a price that would make mining the coal a successful venture. I am told that there is a possibility that this sort of thing


could develop in the next few years, and I have every reason to believe that the power situation in the northwestern United States is such that the people in the area would be glad to get power from such a source as I have mentioned, especially if the conversion of the coal into power can be accomplished at a reasonable price. Therefore we might perhaps see some such thing as that.
Let us suppose for a minute that the Alberta government, interested and very much concerned as it is in the question of helping the coal industry of the province, should make the efforts that they think should be made to encourage the building of great power plants in and near the coal fields. Let us also suppose that some arrangement could be worked out with the northwestern United States power pool to buy the electrical power and that we get the whole thing worked up to the point where agreements are about to be signed. I am going to ask the minister just how far the government of the province of Alberta could go without running into a very rigid federal policy.

I ask you, Mr. Chairman, what better national policy there could be than to adopt those measures which would in very deed make Canadian coal competitive with imported United States coal? But the fact of the matter is that subventions have not done so, and the best evidence of that is that we continue to import into Canada a very large tonnage of United States coal each year. What we ask for when we ask for a national coal policy is a policy that, in very deed, will make it possible for Canadian producers, no matter where they are, to compete favourably with imported coal. What is the harm then, what is the sin, in asking for a national fuel policy? Well, of course my hon. friend, as I said before, criticizes us particularly because he carries around a political chip on his shoulder all the time. He seems to feel that he has enemies around here.
He very wisely made the statement this morning that the coal industry is suffering because of the development of gas and oil. But he then tries to hook on to that this further statement, that he did not think that


it would seem reasonable for the provincial government of Alberta to try to sidestep its responsibilities with regard to coal simply by calling for a national fuel policy. And then, a little later on, he went on to say that the Alberta government are doing something about coal. Then he paid tribute to them for what they are doing.
I point out to the minister that the federal government, by virtue of the fact that they have accepted certain definite responsibilities in connection with mines and technical surveys, and coal, have upon them the obligation to develop a national fuel policy. We are discussing right now, as a matter of fact, item No. 237 which deals with the dominion coal board, and I notice that the minister is asking us-we are not asking him, he is asking us-to give him $10,365,014 to administer the national coal policy. And when we ask that there be a policy, one which no province in Canada by itself could possibly lay down and carry out, from the very nature of our federal arrangement, we run into this difficulty, that the minister turns around and says he thinks it is unreasonable for a provincial government like that of Alberta to try to sidestep its responsibility with regard to coal by simply calling for a national fuel policy. I point out to the minister that the province of Alberta is not attempting to sidestep its responsibility or to throw it off on to him, or anybody else. But we do ask that, when the government or people of this country put up several millions of dollars a year for the administration of a fuel policy, they be given that policy.
That is the whole story. We feel that we have a right to ask for it and that he has no excuse for dragging it into the gutter of politics.

I listened with a great deal of interest to a number of speeches on the coal industry of Canada and I have every sympathy with the members who are concerned with the difficulties. I must congratulate the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond particularly, whose speech was the product of a trained mind, and who speaks with exactitude and uses language with precision. I enjoyed it very much indeed.
I just want to take two or three minutes to bring to the attention of the committee the fact that we have a number of mining communities in the southeastern section of British Columbia that are suffering from a depression as the result of a drop in the price of base metals. These communities were built up as a result of early day exploration and this has resulted in the investment of large amounts of capital in mines, in communities and in public services.
I do wish to bring to the attention of the minister the fact that the companies, trade unions, and communities concerned are very anxious that he frequently nudge the elbows of his colleagues to make certain that this situation is kept under review and that everything be done that can be done to protect the interests of these people.
I am going to read briefly from a resolution I have received and then conclude, Mr. Chairman. This is the opinion of a good many organizations in the district:
The Slocan district board of trade is greatly concerned over the possibility of the United States government imposing a higher tariff on lead and zinc entering the United States.
It costs as much to produce these metals in this area as it does in the western states and we are already paying 0-75 cents a pound duty for lead and 0-6 cents a pound duty for zinc.
Any increase in the tariff would cause further hardship in an area which is already depressed due to the low price of these metals, and would certainly delay the re-opening of several properties which are hoping to operate in the near future.
We strongly urge that the government of Canada make every effort to see that Canada is not placed in the same category as those countries which are in a position to dump these metals at low prices, due to the fact that they do not pay wages near the level enjoyed by American and Canadian workmen.

Then I have a letter here from one of the local unions. They are asking for governmental attention to this question and government support, and are urging that if necessary the government take retaliatory measures, if the Americans increase the tariffs on these metals, by increasing the charges to the United States on such desirable Canadian natural resources as nickel, asbestos, uranium and any other which lends itself to that purpose.
I bring this to the attention of the minister because I promised the organizations concerned to mention it in the house before this session closed. I do urge the minister to use every means in his power to protect the interests of the mining communities concerned, and if necessary by the imposition of duties on the products suggested.

There are two minerals produced in the province of Ontario which deserve a brief mention at this time. The first is natural gas. It may be thought by many hon. members that, because of the vast natural gas fields in western Canada, those are the only sources of natural gas in Canada. The fact is that Ontario is a very old producer and is still producing natural gas, and is discovering new fields every year. The recent discoveries of natural gas in southwestern Ontario indicate a supply which will be of considerable importance in the domestic market. I raise this, Mr. Chairman, because the minister is concerned with natural gas which crosses provincial boundaries, and my point deals with the protection of the local producers of natural gas which would seem to be the concern of both this government and the government of Ontario. Recently arrangements were made to import natural gas across the Niagara frontier and at Windsor in very substantial quantities, and I understand that substantial contracts have been made with the Union Gas Company Limited which is the main distributing agency in that area. I think the two governments who bear the responsibility in this matter should attempt to secure for the local producers of natural gas a fair share of the market when these substantial quantities of imported gas, both from the south and in due course, we hope, from western Canada, become available; otherwise the development of the many undiscovered gas pools in Ontario will be retarded and the industry stifled.
The other mineral with which I wish to deal is gold, and the provisions made under the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act are, of course, a saving factor in that situation. I shall not take the time to go into the
25, 1954	6722
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys problem in detail. My concern is mainly with the gold producers of Ontario, and the fact is that of the 78 gold mines which were producing in 1939 only one-third are in operation today. As everyone knows, that is due to the double handicap of the reduction in the price of gold which they mine, amounting to $4 per ounce or 11 per cent, and the increase, on the other hand, in the cost of production, materials and labour. The cost of materials between 1940 and 1953 ranged from a 48 per cent increase in the cost of dynamite, to 246 per cent increase in the cost of spruce planking used in the mines. In the same way the cost of paper used in the mining industry rose in the same period by 100 per cent. The position of the gold producers compared with the producers of other metals is quite striking. Nickel has enjoyed an increase in price of 29 cents to 57 cents, or an increase of 97 per cent; newsprint has increased by 152 per cent, and other natural products have increased in proportion, so that this problem which has been recognized by the provision of a statutory subsidy in these estimates is one which I am sure will not be overlooked by the minister in the immediate future.
I am not one of those who believe that this condition will continue. I am confident that gold, as a monetary base, will assume its former position in due course as the basis for a broadened international trade, and I am confident that a new price, in conformity with its scarcity value and its proper relationship to other prices, will be re-established. It is significant that in March of this year the buying and selling of gold on the open market after a lapse of 15 years was resumed in London, and there are many other factors which indicate that a monetary system based on gold was one of the casualties of the war. I think that socialistic experiments will in due course be found necessary in any broadened international trade picture.
I am not going to labour that point because much business remains to be done. But I did want to make that passing reference in order to assure the minister that the Ontario producers of both these minerals are watching developments with interest.

speechtext: I should like to take this opportunity of pointing out to the committee the great importance of a new metal which is being developed in this country. I have in mind its great importance in the light of new developments in the aircraft industry with the advent of the jet engine. I refer, of course, to titanium. It is a metal that has not been used commercially to any great extent up until now but it has properties which are suitable for new developments in the design of high performance jet engines. I wonder whether the minister could make a brief statement as to what progress his department is making with regard to the concentration, analysis and reduction of titanium, especially with reference to the deposits in eastern Quebec.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys

speechtext:
I have here a report from the deputy minister which I think will cover what my hon. friend is asking for.
The Department of Mines and Technical Surveys has been instrumental in bringing together all phases of a potential titanium industry in Canada. Total annual titanium requirements in Canada are at present negligible but it is estimated that by 1960 Canada will be able to support a titanium industry about one-tenth the size of the United States industry. The largest Canadian use for titanium metal would be in aircraft manufacture.
Mines branch has assessed the technical practicability of the various titanium production methods being contemplated in Canada and has supplied the Department of Defence Production with data which might be of assistance in formulating policies with regard to government encouragement of the development of a Canadian titanium industry. The branch has given technical assistance to both Dominion Magnesium Limited, and Shawin-igan Water & Power Company during the development of their respective processes. The quality of the titanium produced by each process has been evaluated.
Primary or sponge titanium now sells for from $4.50 to $5.00 a pound in the United States. Under the pressure of competition and by taking full advantage of technical advancements, the currently-used Kroll process could probably produce primary titanium to sell for $3.50 a pound. Shawinigan estimates that a plant using its electrolytic process could produce titanium at a rate of
1,000	tons per year to sell for about $3 per pound. The Shawinigan process is a distinctly Canadian development and would use titanium raw material from Canadian ores. However, it has only been proven on a large laboratory scale, 4 pounds per day per cell. There are admitted unknowns to be encountered in expanding the scale of operations ten times, a step necessary for commercial operations. The government is assisting Shawinigan in the preliminary stages of this expansion.
The mines branch has a broad titanium research program well in hand. This program covers all phases from the treatment of Canadian titanium ores through purification of the metal to melting, alloying, forging, and casting of titanium. Knowledge gained during this program will be available to any Canadian industry engaged in titanium processing or use.
