In connection with marketing service administration-perhaps my comments could come under this item or under a floor price item-I should like to draw the attention of the parliamentary assistant to a situation which was created in the east last year. Quite frankly, I believe it reflects on the marketing administration. There was an agreement entered into, to which the department was at least a party, with respect to a marketing scheme for Prince Edward Island potatoes. Subsequently, owing to the efforts of New Brunswick members, that scheme was enlarged to embrace the potato growers of New Brunswick. With respect to that, we have no complaint whatever. I think the members from both New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island deserve consideration, and undoubtedly they negotiated a proper agreement and one which, in so far as possible, safeguarded their interests.
Unfortunately, at least in so far as the scheme with respect to Prince Edward Island was concerned which was the first one and perhaps was not based on the same experience as the New Brunswick scheme, there was no provision made to provide for orderly marketing. In order to get the price that was guaranteed the growers had to get rid of their crop before a certain date, and no restrictions whatever were placed on them. As a result the growers moved the potatoes into the most available market, the market which naturally appealed to them, and that was the Nova Scotia market where everyone would like to move if they had the opportunity. Since the Prince Edward Island personnel could not move there, they moved their production and flooded the Halifax market with potatoes to such an extent that the Nova Scotia growers suffered very heavy losses. Frankly, I think somebody slipped in that connection.

Supply-Agriculture
I can remember not too many years ago when a marketing arrangement was entered into between the apple growers of Nova Scotia and the dominion government. It was not actually a marketing arrangement, but it was an arrangement into which the government entered and one of the conditions of that arrangement was that the Nova Scotia grower could not ship any apples to either Ontario or Quebec during the growing season. In other words, the growers in Ontario and Quebec were receiving some protection because of the fact that the Nova Scotia grower received some moneys from the dominion treasury. I feel the same principle should have been followed with respect to the marketing of potatoes. I want to bring that to the attention of the parliamentary assistant.
I know the parliamentary assistant is conversant with it, because the matter caused a great many headaches and many discussions. I have a file a foot thick with respect to it, containing complaints from Nova Scotia growers. I reiterate that we have no objection to any agreement entered into with the Prince Edward Island growers or the New Brunswick growers, but there should have been a stipulation attached to that contract that would not have allowed them to dump, because that is what they did, their production in Nova Scotia. They dumped these potatoes into the Halifax market and Prince Edward Island potatoes were selling far below the cost of production and shipment from the Annapolis valley to that market. The same thing happened to a lesser extent in Ontario and Quebec. There were protests from Ontario and Quebec growers with respect to that. To put it mildly, it was not an intelligent deal. As a matter of fact, to express it frankly, it was a stupid deal, and one which I believe the department should watch very carefully in future. In making marketing agreements we should see that, as a result, we do not create a disorderly market instead of an orderly market.

Since the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings has referred to this potato situation I may say there has been considerable controversy in Ontario regarding it. I did have some correspondence with the chairman of the prices support board and I believe that the situation will be ironed out in another year. It did cause considerable concern amongst the Ontario and Quebec growers, but since the situation has been pointed out by the Ontario potato producers organization I hope something will be done about it before another year. I think I mentioned before, when the minister was here, that there seems to be a considerable

amount of difference between the postage and telephone rates in all the items. I wonder if the parliamentary assistant can explain the difference this year as compared with last year.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to support what previous speakers have mentioned with regard to the marketing of potatoes last year. I have no doubt representations have been made to the parliamentary assistant, because he represents Middlesex West, which is a good potato growing area.
As I have said all along, the price support program has been a dismal failure. And it has been a failure so far as the potato growers in Ontario are concerned, because the maritimers were subsidized and allowed to bring potatoes into Ontario.
Please excuse Nova Scotia.

It might be Nova Scotia next year. If the program does not apply to the whole crop right across Canada, then the result is that one group of people is paying to subsidize the other. I suggest that is not a satisfactory way to do it. I have no doubt the parliamentary assistant is aware of this situation and will probably take care of it.

Since New Brunswick potatoes have been brought into the picture I think I should say just a few words. The hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings, from Nova Scotia, and the hon. member who has spoken from Ontario, may be dissatisfied, and I think they have some grounds for their complaint. I think, too, that during the last season the department learned a good many lessons in this connection.
To be quite frank about it, I am inclined to be in favour of the present program. At least theoretically, to my mind it is a good thing. I come from a constituency which is known as one of the greatest potato growing areas in Canada, one which depends almost entirely upon the potato crop. It is clear that when people must depend upon one particular commodity to sustain their economy they are in great difficulty when something goes wrong.
Down my way certainly the people are not all happy, but there are some who are. I am in hopes that the department has learned its lesson. If such an agreement is entered into in another year I believe all the provinces asking for the agreement should start off on a target date. In other words, one province should not be allowed to enter the agreement before another and start selling its potatoes earlier. While Nova Scotia may have a complaint, we certainly had one

during the fall and previous to January 1954. Because, as soon as the Prince Edward Island board entered the picture, they knocked the price down on the market. This meant that anyone else who tried to arrange steady and orderly marketing could not do so. However, when New Brunswick came on the market under a board, Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick boards co-operated. If Nova Scotia wants to enter the picture with Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick they will have to have a board.
I think it should be insisted upon that a certain date be fixed at which all boards will begin to operate. So long as any one board is operating separately there will be some difficulty.
Then there is another point I would like to mention. This spring in my area there were a few farmers left with practically 90 per cent of their potatoes on hand, either in their cellars or in their potato houses. They just could not get rid of them, although they had signed up with the board. Only a few days ago I received a letter from a man who still had 90 per cent of his potatoes, and who claims he signed up early in the winter. However, the board has never called for any of his potatoes. This man is only one of a certain number who find themselves in that position. They have to take a loss, because they get nothing unless they deliver their potatoes to the board. On the other hand, those who got rid of their potatoes received more money than if they had been operating on a free market.
It may be urged that this matter is outside the jurisdiction of the federal Department of Agriculture, and that may be true. I suggest however that the federal department might use considerable influence, and if the growers want a floor price, the department could say to them, "You must take the potatoes from the farmers on a percentage basis, similar to that which obtains in connection with wheat deliveries in the western provinces, where they take so many bushels per acre." In this way one farmer would not be able to sell three or four thousand barrels of potatoes while another has to hold his until the following April or May.
Anyone who knows anything about the potato business knows very well that after May 10 potatoes shrink very quickly, unless they are in a very cool potato house. Once that starts the inspector comes along, and there is tremendous shrinkage. You find you cannot sell your potatoes, because we know that the consumers will not buy potatoes that are shrivelled and sprouted. Once potatoes have sprouts about ten inches long they lose their flavour and will not sell. So it is important that every farmer be treated
Supply-Agriculture
as nearly as possible in the same way, so that everything would be sold through a marketing board.
I am wondering if Ontario really suffered very much. Had a board been set up in this province I doubt very much whether they would have been guaranteed a price greater than would have been in line with the cost of production and the movement of their potatoes to the market in Ontario. I doubt very much if they lost money because boards are operating in the maritime provinces. And before I take my seat I would draw the attention of people in Ontario who are producing potatoes, or producing anything else, to the terms of confederation which state that we are to have some preference when entering this market.
The parliamentary assistant has not answered my question concerning postage and telephones.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I intend to answer, but I have been listening to the potato discussion, and I wished to deal with all those subjects when I spoke. I will not forget what the hon. member has asked.
I believe that is the end of the potato discussion.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
As the hon. member for Middlesex East has said, I come from a potato growing district. Many of the farmers in my constituency produce potatoes. The criticism I have heard from three hon. members is one I have heard in my own riding. In Ontario we could have come under a cooperative marketing plan, just as Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick have. Nova Scotia could have done so, too. Unfortunately in Ontario this year we have not done that. The result has been that potatoes have been coming into Ontario from those other two provinces and depressing our market. Our potato growers do not like that. It is hard to overcome, of course, unless we have a potato marketing scheme of our own -which we hope we will have in other years. It was my privilege just a few months ago to go down to North Carolina, in the United States, which is a great potato-growing state, as hon. members know. In that state there is a market for a lot of the maritime potatoes. They like our potatoes. I was glad to hear them say they liked the potatoes that come from the maritime provinces. The committee knows that 95 per cent of the seed in that state comes from Prince Edward Island, which speaks well for the potato growers of that province. That is the way we like it, but nevertheless in that state I heard the same criticism that is heard here, that some

Supply-Agriculture
other states farther west were growing potatoes and shipping them over their borders and depressing their markets. The problems that we have here are the problems that they have down in the United States as well.
Of course we like to have interprovincial trade even though it sometimes hurts us; but we hope, as the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings mentioned, that next year we shall be able to work it out on a better basis even though we did suffer during the past year.

31. Agricultural economics, $630,153.

Perhaps I should have dealt with this when the hon. member for Kootenay West asked his question about apples, but I thought it came more directly under agricultural economics. On June 11, I asked the Minister of Trade and Commerce a question about the likelihood of our getting a substantial order in re-entering the United Kingdom market for apples, because I had noticed press reports to the effect that the United Kingdom had indicated they were able to allocate dollars for the purchase of cheese. That indicates that as a result of the improvement in their economic situation over there they should be able to become once again a substantial purchaser of food from this continent. That certainly is our hope. I understand it is theirs. However, the Minister of Trade and Commerce said in answer to the question on June 11, as reported at page 5829 of Hansard:
So far as fruits are concerned, we have had an indication that the United Kingdom is allocating dollars to cover purchase of certain canned fruits, but negotiations regarding apples are still in progress.
That was confirmed by what the parliamentary assistant has just said to the hon. member for Kootenay West, as I understood the answer. Since the United Kingdom is again becoming a potential market for Canadian agricultural produce, there is no group of agricultural producers in this country more interested in re-entering that market than the apple producers, and particularly those of British Columbia, I venture to say, to whom that market was more important than to any others. Perhaps my hon. friend from Nova Scotia might say it was equally important to them, but certainly it was very important to the apple producers of our province. In the discussions with the United Kingdom, is anything being said or done with respect to obtaining some concessions on the tariff treatment accorded to Canadian apples? The parliamentary assistant will remember that up until 1947 or
[Mr. McCubbin.l
1948 we enjoyed a preferential tariff with the British market which was abandoned. Coincidentally with the abandonment of that preferential tariff, the British stopped buying anyway because of the shortage of dollars. The indications are now that they will be a potential apple-buying country. Is anything being done to restore to us that advantageous position in the British market which was of such great benefit to our apple producers?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Every avenue that can be explored is being explored. That market has been a good one in years gone by for British Columbia apples as well as Nova Scotia apples, and we hope it will be some time in the future, and I hope that the future is not too far away. I am sorry I cannot give a more favourable reply, but I am always optimistic. Unfortunately I cannot give any better reply at this time.

Perhaps the parliamentary assistant does know what lines of approach are being taken by the Canadian delegations. Were any instructions issued to them on the basis of which we shall be able to say we are exploring this line or that line?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Every avenue that can be explored is being explored. We are doing that.
Are we justified in assuming from that that this line of approach is being pursued?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Yes, every avenue.
I want to ask the parliamentary assistant a question about the cheese deal with Great Britain this year. Has he anything to say about that?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I am sorry; I cannot give an answer to my hon. friend except that he knows as well as I do that the Ontario people are over there right now and are trying to enter into negotiations with the British for the purchase of Canadian cheese. We have not had any report from them as yet.
I hope that the dominion Department of Agriculture and the dominion government are doing more to help the Ontario producers this year than they did last year to sell the cheese.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: They will help them every year.
They did not help last year.

I do not intend to enter into any discussion on this matter of agricultural economics, although frankly I was the one

who asked to have it stand over because I knew that the hon. member for Kamloops had something to bring up. I also had something I wanted to raise at this time. I do not think now is the opportune time to do it because of the schedule under which we are working.
We have until the end of next week.

I should like to add a word to what the hon. member for Kamloops and the hon. member for Kootenay West have already said about the British Columbia apple industry. The minister is fully aware that for the last thirty years our apple industry has been geared up to the United Kingdom demand for apples. We pruned trees, planted varieties and did everything we could to meet the demands of that market, and that was done at the original suggestion of the federal government. We carried out their wishes to the best of our ability to produce the exact type of apples they wanted in the United Kingdom. I understand the situation today is that the British people like our apples very much, but before they can import them they require some sort of concession on the part of the Canadian government whereby there will be a balance of trade. Does the parliamentary assistant know if any concession has been offered with a view to regaining the market in Britain for apples? One other question. In connection with the negotiations now taking place, is there a member of the fruit industry from British Columbia taking part in these negotiations?

44. Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act and water storage, $3,899,245.

Mr. Chairman, just before this item is carried I might just say that I do not want to enter into another discussion this afternoon on the P.F.R.A. and I do not intend to say anything controversial at this point. I simply want to say that I was in western Canada last week and visited my own constituency for a few days. As hon. members know, that is the constituency that would be most affected favourably by the Saskatchewan river dam project. I merely wish to tell the government this afternoon, though I observe there is no minister present and, of course, the parliamentary assistant does not attend the meetings of the cabinet-
There is one minister here.

I did not notice the Secretary of State, but perhaps he will be able to carry my message. I want to tell the minister that, having just returned from my own constituency, I know there is considerable disappointment at recent statements that have been made in regard to this project. I want to say on behalf of my constituents that they hope that consideration will be given to this matter in the near future so that it can be proceeded with without delay. It may be said at the moment that irrigation is not necessary. I quite agree that, with some farms under three to six feet of water, it does not seem to be the time to be discussing irrigation. But those of us who have lived in western Canada for 40 years or more, as some of us have done, know there are periods when there is dry, drought weather, which involve the country in very large expenditures for feed and for the relief of the stricken population. It seems to me that, when we have wet years, that is the time to prepare for the dry years which must inevitably follow. I do not wish to discuss this subject in a controversial manner this afternoon or to argue once again in favour of it, but all I would simply say

through the parliamentary assistant, or the Secretary of State, if you like, is that the people I represent in this house are very anxious to have this matter settled and proceeded with. They feel the provincial government has made a generous offer to bear a large part of the expenditure, indeed larger than I anticipated the province would or should be called upon to bear, but that offer has been made and they are prepared to stand by it. I am taking this opportunity, perhaps the last opportunity this session, to express the hope that serious consideration will be given to this project and that it will be undertaken in the near future.

Mr. Chairman, I hesitate to delay the committee at this period of the session but this matter is of such importance to the people of Saskatchewan that I think hon. members will forgive me if I take a few moments to deal with it, especially in view of the fact that it is several years since I have spoken on this matter in this house. Members will have seen the answer which was given to the question I asked of the ministry and which was reported in yesterday's Hansard, and that answer discloses a situation which I would like to draw to the attention of the government.
I am aware of the fact that the Prime Minister and the government have taken the attitude that they will recommend this South Saskatchewan river dam project if they are satisfied that the required expenditure is warranted as in the public interest. I would like to say that it is the attitude, certainly at least of the majority of the people of Saskatchewan, that they can have great faith in the fairness of the Prime Minister and the present government. They are satisfied that if and when a case is made out for the construction of this project it will be unhesitatingly proceeded with. It is in that spirit that I make these few remarks this afternoon.
Does the hon. member think a case has been made out? I am quite sure he does.

As far as I am concerned, I am satisfied that the project should be proceeded with, but I realize that we must convince the people of the other nine provinces of Canada, and it is with that idea in mind that I speak. I feel that if we can place the facts before our fellow citizens in the other provinces of Canada and the Prime Minister and prove that we have a good case then I have no doubt as to what the decision will be.
The answer to the question I asked yesterday discloses a situation which must lead

our people to ask themselves how the problem it discloses is to be met. 1 asked what the population of Canada was according to the census of 1941, and I then asked what the estimated population was now, and for the population of the various provinces in 1941 and now according to the latest estimates. The answer I received is to be found at page 6609 of Hansard and it reveals that the population of Canada as of June 2, 1941, excluding Newfoundland, was 11,506,655. The estimated population as of June 1, 1953, was 14,398,000, also excluding Newfoundland. That shows that our country had had a splendid increase in population during that time, and an increase that should make every Canadian gratified. We had an increase, without considering Newfoundland, of 25-6 per cent. In other words, in that period of a little bit over a decade our population had increased by one-quarter. But when one looks at the population of Saskatchewan, instead of our sharing in that great development in which we all take such pride we find that our province's population has decreased during that period by 3 per cent. It is the only province in Canada which had a decrease during that period.
That is because they have a C.C.F. government.
That is not the reason, and the hon. member knows it.

It is pointed out that there is a C.C.F. government there and that that is the reason for lack of development. But I am also saying that other things should be taken into consideration as having to do with that situation.
During that same period Prince Edward Island had an increase in population of 11-5 per cent; Nova Scotia, 14-7 per cent; New Brunswick, 17-2 per cent; Quebec, 28-1 per cent; Ontario, 29-3 per cent; Manitoba, 10-9 per cent; Saskatchewan, as I say, had a decrease of 3-9 per cent. Alberta had an increase of 25-9 per cent; British Columbia, an increase of 50-4 per cent; Yukon, an increase of 83-2 per cent; Northwest Territories, an increase of 33 per cent. There is the picture of our growth that I think every Canadian should look at. If there is anything that can be done by the federal government to see to it that Saskatchewan shares with the rest of the country in that great forward march, I think it should be done. I am sure that everybody in all the rest of the provinces of Canada would be ready to do anything within reason to help us to share in that development. When it is remembered that every other single province has had a tremendous increase in population, that our
Supply-Agriculture
country as a whole has had an increase of 25 per cent, and that we in Saskatchewan have gone back during that period of the greatest development our country has ever known so far as population is concerned, it seems to me that we have a case to put before not only this government but the provincial government.
A royal commission was set up to make an investigation into this matter. I do not intend at this time to go into this matter otherwise than to suggest a few important points. The royal commission considered the question of irrigation and the advantages of irrigation. I would point out that, from that standpoint, there is a strong case to be made out for the construction of this as an irrigation system. It can irrigate about half a million acres. In periods of drought those half million acres would produce feed and fodder which would help to maintain our livestock industry in a substantial part of the province. That result in itself, outside of the increased production on irrigated lands, would have, in stabilizing our agriculture, an effect which it is hard to estimate.
Any farmer who went through the period of the drought in the thirties and who had perhaps spent almost a lifetime in building up a herd of valuable cattle knows what happened. It got to the point where the dominion government, to try to help us out, was even fetching in fodder from as far away as Nova Scotia. Obviously the attitude had to be taken that as much livestock should be disposed of as possible. The farmers had to dispose of cattle at as low as one cent a pound. Herds were practically wiped out and the savings and work of hardworking people disappeared because of what happened. Had there been a place in the province, 500,000 acres in extent, which could have been put to growing fodder and feed, that situation would not have needed to develop.
The farmers in Saskatchewan realize that, while we are having plenty of rain today, just as sure as they live in that great central plain, drought will come again. They also realize that if nothing fundamental is done, they are going to be up against the same difficulty again, that of not having feed and fodder for their herds. That realization has a deterring effect upon the building up of our mixed farming industry in Saskatchewan.
Surely if we want to increase our population we must encourage our people to go into mixed farming and not to go more and more into the field of bigger and bigger grain farms. When the latter course is followed, it means, of course, that farm people have to go elsewhere in order to make a living as

Supply-Agriculture
farms get bigger and bigger, and bigger machinery is used. The people in the rest of Canada I am sure are deeply interested in seeing to it that the farming population of Saskatchewan is not cut down year by year because, of course, in the long run that cut will also mean that the urban population of Saskatchewan will begin to diminish.
There is another angle to the irrigation problem. There are people who need to be settled upon land. Irrigation would provide farms upon which we could resettle many people who are today looking for land. It would help in that regard. So much for the advantage of the scheme from the irrigation standpoint.
Then there is the question of electric power. The province of Saskatchewan today is engaged on a program of farm electrification. Last year I think they connected almost
6,000	farmers with electricity. While I was in the legislature out there, I unceasingly took the attitude that if we were going to halt the trend of farmers away from the farms and into the cities, we had to give the people on the farms the same amenities of life and the same comforts as they would have if they lived in the city. One of the ways in which that may be done is by having electricity on the farms.
The government of Saskatchewan has embarked upon an energetic farm electrification program which I advocated strongly and which I am glad to see now being gone ahead with. We are told that 75,000 farms in Saskatchewan can be connected economically with electricity. That program not only will tend to keep people happily on the farms but it will also promote mixed farming. It will make it more profitable. It will make mixed farming more efficient and it will make it possible to do it more economically. If we can in that way halt the trend away from the country and into the cities, and halt the trend away from mixed farming to large grain farming, by constructing this dam project thereby making electricity available more cheaply-and especially when the provincial government is ready to pay the cost of that feature of it-surely it is something that should be done. But it cannot be done unless the dam is put in there. That is an important consideration.
There is also the matter of industrial development. We realize that the reason why some other provinces have gone ahead so fast is that they have benefited by great industrial development. To have industrial development you need minerals and electricity. You need gas, perhaps; but above all, you need plenty of water for most modern industrial processes. In most of the settled area of
fMr. Tucker.]
Saskatchewan there is not a large constant supply of water. It looks as though we have plenty of natural gas to provide for a great increase and expansion in industry. But, in order to have that increase, we need to have plenty of water for industrial purposes. That is a feature that I think was not given due weight in the report of the royal commission. The royal commission dealt with the question of irrigation and dealt with the question of electricity. They dealt with those two items mainly, but they did not deal with the social value of this project from the standpoint of laying the foundation for the overall expansion and development of our province.
So far as the question of developing electricity and irrigation is concerned, it is quite true that for some time the project perhaps will not much more than pay interest on the capital invested by the federal government. I think that it will do that in a very short time after it is completed. I think the studies showed that the increase in agricultural production would amount to at least $6 million in value, taking the value of that production at average prices for farm products over a long term. The way things stand today I think we can look for prices not to go back to the low level of previous years, but even with that conservative estimate the increase in value of agricultural production would be at least $6 million. I think it also is the experience that if you have an increase in the income of your farmers by $6 million it will lead to an over-all increase in the income of other people by at least twice that amount, which suggests that at the very minimum the increase in production as the result of this irrigation project would be at least $18 million.
About 20 per cent of the national income is paid in taxes, and 20 per cent of $18 million would amount to $3-6 million. If you consider what the dominion would have to spend on the project, even assuming that it would be far more than the amount of $70 million envisaged by the last conference of experts, even supposing that the dominion would have to spend $100 million, with the government getting their money at approximately 3-J per cent the amount of $3-6 million I have just mentioned will carry the interest on $100 million. That is from the irrigation aspect alone. On top of that you have to consider that there will be cheaper electricity and plenty of water provided right in the midst of the settled area of Saskatchewan which is bound to lead to a tremendous industrial expansion because we have the other necessary element the minerals there.

We have 80,000 square miles of the PreCambrian shield right in Saskatchewan. This is the same shield, the same mineral formation, that is providing the iron in Labrador, the same formation that has resulted in the establishment of various mines in northern Manitoba and Ontario.
If Saskatchewan could get electricity and plenty of water, instead of being the weak link in the development of our country it would, I am satisfied, become one of Canada's soundest and strongest links. That is a feature to which I suggest the royal commission did not give enough attention, the effect that the project would have upon the industrial development of our province.
As I said at the outset, I do not intend to impose on the good will of the committee at this particular moment, but I suggest that we recognize the fact that in the past hundred years we have had at least three bad periods of drought in western Canada. I have been told by people who went into that area in the nineties that it was so dry that there were cracks in the ground into which a horse's leg would go. I went through the period of drought in the thirties. If hon. members had seen what some people had to go through during that period they would certainly want to do something about it so that when drought comes again, as come it will, the people of that part of Saskatchewan will feel that their fellow citizens in the rest of Canada have taken concrete steps to try to protect them against a recurrence of the worst effects of that terrible experience.
The people of Saskatchewan appreciated the attitude of the rest of Canada in providing them with help during the last drought period, not only help in the form of grants of money but in supplying them with vegetables and other things to help them over that difficult period. But the people of Saskatchewan would like the people of the rest of Canada to take steps to enable them to fight what lies ahead themselves without having to ask for assistance.
Hear, hear.

That is what I say to my fellow citizens of the rest of Canada. You were generous when we needed help in the thirties. You did not hesitate to put through a very fine measure of help in the form of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act to protect our farmers in the event of drought. This has been a great thing for the farmers of western Canada. We have one of the finest systems any place in the world under P.F.R.A. of bringing light land under grass, providing small irrigation schemes, dugouts and so on. I have been told by people who have some
Supply-Agriculture
experience in these matters that the P.F.R.A. scheme put into effect by the people of Canada for western Canada is one of the finest in the whole world.
The scheme I am now suggesting will cost quite a bit more than any of these other projects, but with Canada strong financially and in every other way, with Canada still rapidly growing in strength and having in mind the things that we could do in the thirties and forties, surely we can say now that here is a scheme that will provide a really solid foundation which will carry and supplement these other things if we run into a bad drought again. I suggest that the saving by the irrigation of the land alone in respect of the P.F.A.A. will amount to close to half a million dollars a year on the average. A saving of that proportion will be well worth while in helping to pay the cost of carrying this dam proposition.
Oh, oh.

I know that it is already referred to in that way by a lot of people in western Canada. I hope that it is regarded otherwise here-as something in connection with which we may look to our fellow citizens of the rest of Canada with confidence. We take pride in what is being done in other parts of Canada. Now, above all, western Canada takes great pride in the fact that Canada said that, if necessary, she would go it alone on the St. Lawrence seaway proposition, that she would no longer be held up by the unwillingness of the United States to participate. I say, Mr. Chairman, that far away as we are from the St. Lawrence, there was no place in all Canada where there was more approval of that attitude of the government of our country than there was right in Saskatchewan.
We are great supporters of the idea of the development of our country. The people of Saskatchewan, coming as they do from pretty well all parts of the western world, have become a group of people who have a very firm devotion to Canada as their country. The people of Saskatchewan are 100 per cent behind anything they see that will help Canada to stand on its own feet, anything that is necessary to lay the foundation for an even greater country. All we ask is that the people of Canada generally look at our situation and realize clearly that we do not want to be the weak link in the chain of the development of our country in an agricultural way, with the possibility of another drought hanging over our heads. All we ask is that our fellow Canadians realize that we are not experiencing the great development that is being experienced in the rest of Canada, that our sons and daughters are

Supply-Agriculture
having to leave Saskatchewan and go elsewhere to make a living, that our population is going down while that of the rest of the country is going up. We say to the rest of Canada: We rejoice in your prosperity and development but give us a chance to pull our weight. If you will give us that chance you will have reason to be proud of Saskatchewan just as Saskatchewan is proud of Canada.

Mr. Chairman, I cannot very well refrain from saying a word or two in this discussion since my own city is the city which, of all cities in Canada, would benefit most from the proposed dam. I too am not going into any controversial aspects of the question, and I congratulate the hon. member for Rosthern on the very good speech he has made. I am glad to hear he is totally in favour of the project. We will have to change the minds of some of the people of Canada and we will have to change the mind of the Prime Minister. While I do not agree with him, may I say that I admire the honesty and integrity of the statement the Prime Minister made when he said that he did not yet see that the national interest would be served by this amount of money on this particular project. I think that is an honest attitude. The only thing to which I have ever objected in the speeches that have been made by hon. members on the other side of the house is that this project has been used, I am afraid, as political bait before elections. I believe the Prime Minister's forthright statement previous to the last election, and it was an honest statement, has done much to clear the air in that regard.
I was afraid the hon. member for Rosthern was going to get off the track on which he had promised to keep when one of his colleagues interjected something about the population of Saskatchewan having decreased because we had a C.C.F. government there. Both the hon. member who made the interjection and my hon. friend who, for the last five or six years, has been fighting that government, know perfectly well that is not true.

If my hon. friend says I know that quite well, I will not accept it because I believe that, if it had not been for the fear of that government during at least its first two years, private capital would have entered the province and we would have had a greater development than we have.
There was a drop in population before the C.C.F. government took office.
My hon. friend was going to leave politics out of it.

I did not mention it until my friend suggested I knew something which I did not say. I tell him that I believe the Saskatchewan C.C.F. government has contributed substantially to the failure of our province to develop faster than it has. If my hon. friend wants my belief from me, he gets it; that is what I believe.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for Saskatoon has the floor and cannot be interrupted without his consent.
I rose on a question of privilege. The hon. member suggested I had said something I knew perfectly well was wrong.
I want to say to the hon. member for Rosthern-

I tell him that he himself knows his own city would have had greater development. A big metal smelting plant would have been established in Saskatoon instead of Edmonton if natural gas had been found shortly before it was. The provincial minister of highways said that just the other day.
The Liberals in power found no gas.

What I said was, the hon. gentleman who interjected tried to persuade my hon. friend from Rosthern to adopt the idea that the reason for the decrease in population in Saskatchewan was due to a C.C.F. government, when he knew, and the hon. member for Rosthern knew, that that was not the fact. I did not suggest the hon. member has not always told what he believed upon every occasion upon which he has been attacking the C.C.F. government in Saskatchewan. In so far as this point is concerned, the hon. member has started something and I do not want to continue it. I could talk for 40 minutes on this, if I wanted to do so, but no one wants to hear me and I do not want to do so.
However, the hon. member for Rosthern did say something about Saskatchewan being the weak link in the development of Canada. He said, in rebuttal of what I had suggested, that apparently it was still the weak link in Canada because people could not invest their money as a result of the fear of the Saskatchewan government. I would refer him, therefore, to a survey made by Professor Britnell of the University of Saskatchewan, a man for whom people have the highest respect for his ability as an economist, a man who has gone to foreign countries to assess situations and been

greatly praised for his findings. I find that Professor Britnell, at page 450 of the report, had this to say:
Thus, over a five-year period, annual capital expenditures exactly doubled in Alberta, increased by 71 per cent in Saskatchewan, but-
Why should I read about Manitoba?
Oh, oh.

All right.
... by only 21 per cent in Manitoba, as compared with 61 per cent for the whole country.
I am not suggesting the hon. member for Rosthern does not tell the truth. I am simply giving Dr. Britnell's findings in the economic survey, which, so far as I am concerned, I am prepared to accept. The total investment in Canada from 1948 to 1953 went up by 61 per cent. In Saskatchewan, it went up by 71 per cent, or 10 per cent higher than the national average. I did not intend to start any controversy, but then I do not mind taking on my hon. friend any time either in Saskatchewan or elsewhere. My hon. friend has been doing his best out there for the last six years and now he is back here. I shall say no more about that.
I was going on to say a word about the causes of the decrease in population. I must not say what my hon. friend knows quite well, because he will assert something else. My hon. friend has been playing around too long with the Minister of Agriculture, so he has various answers to fit various occasions. However, everybody knows that the depopulation of Saskatchewan, if indeed it is serious enough to be called that, has been due to the mechanization of the farms. My hon. friend knows that. It is also due to the fact-
Your hon. friend does not know that at all. The same thing has happened in the rest of Canada; so far as mechanization is concerned they have had it too, and their population has gone up.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I must ask the hon. member to allow the hon. member who has the floor to proceed without interruption.
Let him not say that I know something that I do not know. Let him make his own speech.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I do not believe the hon. member has any point of privilege, and therefore the hon. member for Saskatoon should be allowed to proceed.
I am rather pleased that my hon. friend has returned-

Let the hon. member for Saskatoon deal with the matter before us.
Supply-Agriculture

The hon. member has been so quiet these last few months, we have hardly been able to believe it. I am quite intrigued that he is coming back into character. This mechanization did have a serious effect on the population, and it occurred at the time the boys went to the last war. They went to the last war to serve their country, and when they returned from overseas they found the farms mechanized to such an extent there were much larger farms and there was no place for many of them to fit in.
Let me again congratulate my hon. friend upon what he said. I shall not say what he said or did not say, because that is not safe. I do want to say a word about this business of rainfall. Some people have argued that this dam is not necessary because this year we have a lot of water, in fact perhaps too much so far as wheat is concerned. What we need in Saskatchewan to increase our population is a change in the type of farming; that is, to some extent to get away from wheat farming and get to the farming of such things as beet sugar, cattle and all the rest of it.
What rain we have had this year, and we have had plenty, is not yet sufficient for that type of farming. If we had a rainfall which would permit successful mixed farming of that type, to grow beet sugar and the like, it would be so great it would simply ruin our wheat crop. We have to have water, therefore. What we do want is water in a moderately dry climate; water which must be put on that land by artificial means. We will have a new type of farming. I do not believe we will have the same farmers we have now. I doubt very much if the same farmers in Saskatchewan will be willing to get out with a hoe, a shovel and in long rubber boots to push water around the place. They have been on a tractor too long for that.
This whole question ties up with immigration. We will have people, for instance, from Holland, a country that does that sort of work. We can get very good people if we can show them an area where there is irrigation. We would not get them to come there and carry out practices which it had not been their life's work to do. When the Canadian Pacific irrigated the land around the Bow river there was no difficulty whatever in selling the farms at high prices for those days, $75 an acre to people from the United States who had been working on irrigated land. So they came in there and, so far as I know, they have prospered. At any rate they have done their own province of Alberta and Canada as a whole some good. I would like to see more of that sort of thing in Saskatchewan.

Supply-Agriculture
In the circumstances I shall not say more. I must say I was surprised a moment ago to hear that here in the house we are operating tonight on a schedule. I hope that is true, although I am afraid that perhaps it is not. In any case, owing to circumstances, I shall not pursue the argument any further. I hope that from now on this dam will be something to which we can look forward. And if I may take the risk of again incurring the anger of my hon. friend, I would suggest that I hope he or the Minister of Agriculture or any other Liberal speakers from now on will not use this subject any more as political bait, until the head of the government of this country and the cabinet make up their minds that, in all circumstances, this expenditure is justified from the point of view of the good of the whole nation, as I believe it to be.

Mr. Chairman, I am pleased to see this vote for P.F.R.A., but I am sorry that, to date, the government has not seen fit to extend its application to British Columbia. We all realize its excellent advantages more and more as we hear discussions between members from both sides of the house.
For years the farm organizations in British Columbia have been urging the government to extend the terms of this act to British Columbia. And my British Columbia colleague from Kamloops has been foremost in the House of Commons in advocating this same policy. I wish to say that I support that request, and I trust that when these estimates come before us again the legislation will be so amended that there will be provision for this type of work in British Columbia.
Mr. Chairman, I cannot allow this item to pass without making my bow to the hon. member for Kootenay West for the way in which he also has agitated for the extension of this act to British Columbia.

Mr. Chairman, I am not going to carry forward the discussion on the Saskatchewan dam. It is not because I lack interest in it, because I do feel it is very important to all the western provinces. But I would like to bring to the attention of the committee again the problem of conservation and flood control on the Assiniboine river. We do not hear very much about this subject.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That would come under item 50.
I am referring to a P.F.R.A. project.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Item 50 deals with the Assiniboine river, diking and cut-off.

It could come under that item or, I suggest, it could come under this one.
	'

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Go ahead; speak up.

The only time we have any discussion of this subject is during the annual consideration of the estimates. Perhaps the reason we do not hear so much about it is that members from Manitoba are not so vociferous as members from Saskatchewan. This subject has been under consideration since 1886. Last year when I questioned the Minister of Agriculture on the matter he referred me to a report on conservation and flood control on the Assiniboine river that was prepared by the P.F.R.A. branch, and completed and published in December, 1952.
I discover in that report a very comprehensive consideration of the whole problem. I raise this matter at this late hour in the session because throughout the day, today, over the radio I have been hearing that flood conditions on the Assiniboine river have reached the city of Brandon, and that the mayor of that city has requested that a large section of the low-lying area be evacuated.
The last press dispatch I have on the subject, dated Saturday, June 19, appears in the Brandon Daily Sun as follows:
The city works department employees are busily engaged in building temporary dykes and the civil defence committee is preparing emergency accommodation for use in case evacuation of the homes in the threatened area becomes necessary.
That has now become necessary, and once again the flood tide is rolling through the Assiniboine basin. I am sorry the Minister of Agriculture is not here, because he is fully cognizant of the problem. In 1950, when the Assiniboine river last reached flood level, he made a personal visit to the area and examined the situation for himself. The report to which I have referred recommends two major projects in flood control and conservation in the Assiniboine basin. I refer to the Russell reservoir at Russell, Manitoba, and the Portage la Prairie diversion. These two projects are actually proposed in connection with the larger flood program in the city of Winnipeg. Because, as hon. members know, the Assiniboine eventually flows into the Red river at Winnipeg.
I should like to ask just what has been done in regard to the report published in 1952. As I indicated, the minister said last spring when we were considering the estimates that the matter was under consideration. As this condition has been developing from 1886, and has been under consideration since that time, I would hope this year that some specific information might be available as to what the department contemplates in regard to the recommendations of the report.

I should like to say a word or two regarding the Saskatchewan dam

development. I am somewhat in agreement, for a change, with the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre, in what he said the other evening.

subtopic: JOSEPH DELPHIS GUILLAUME DELORME
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I rise for the purpose of making an appeal to certain hon. gentlemen opposite. I listened this morning to the very eloquent words of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre in another context, in which he said he thought it was a queer sort of democracy where one person could say no and deny something to three people who want to say yes. He said in another context that he thought the will of the majority should prevail and the will of the minority should not be allowed to thwart it. It seems to me, sir, that everything that can usefully be said on this bill has already been said and there is no reason why the house should not divide on it and the will of the majority prevail. I appeal to the hon. gentlemen opposite to follow out the precepts that were laid down by their spokesman this morning.

subtopic: JOSEPH DELPHIS GUILLAUME DELORME
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would point out with due respect to the Secretary of State that we on this side of the house know something about private bills; that these divorce bills are not government bills. We know that the Prime Minister has made that abundantly clear upon every occasion upon which he has spoken upon divorce in this house. We on this side of the house have had the experience of moving private bills
Private Bill-Divorce
and we have had the experience of having to put up with the fate that happened to them because some member or two or a dozen on the government side of the house did not agree with our philosophy or perhaps with some particular issue which was the subject of our private bill.
This bill was last considered on Tuesday, and I gave the house due notice then-and I have heard nothing from the Secretary of State except what he has just said now in regard to it-that I was opposed to the passing of this bill; that I proposed to debate that question; that I proposed to show the reasons why I am opposed to the granting of this divorce. Thus it is that I am not likely to bother too much about the evidence which would support the view opposite to my own, and I shall be exceedingly proud-I said "proud", because I know the ability of the Secretary of State as a debater-if he will rise in his place and argue the other side of the case. Let me remind the Secretary of State that the only time-I should not say "the only time", because technically this bill has been before this house four times; but on one occasion at least it did receive some consideration owing to the fact that the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam happened to notice the thing as it passed through the mill. It happened to be a big fat divorce bill-I think that was the term he used-so he thought he would read it. Even after that it passed all these stages. From then on I concluded that this bill should not pass. It was a perfect example of the way this house does not perform its duty in scrutinizing these measures.
Yes, we have this committee of the Senate, of course. It has proven not to be infallible. I said this: I am prepared to debate this bill and I am prepared to debate every bill where I think there is a reasonable chance of killing the bill, provided that there might be injustice involved. I do not say that about bills which are unopposed. I know that in these unopposed bills there is collusion and plenty of it; but where the home is broken up, if these people have agreed to live apart, if they are living apart, if there is no purpose to be served in joining together or trying to join together people who are incompatible, then I am not bothering too much about it. But where there is a woman-and there is a woman in this case-or a man to whom any injustice is done, I shall fight that case and I shall fight every case on the floor of this house, and I shall fight it in the miscellaneous private bills committee.
My hon. friend talks about passing this bill being the will of the majority. I tell him that if every man in this house were taken out behind the curtains and you asked him

Private Bill-Divorce to look you in the eye and say honestly and say from his heart whether he is in favour of the way in which this House of Commons, the Senate and this committee deal with these things, if he is an honest man he will look you in the face and say: I am sick and tired of this rotten thing; let us get it out of the forum of this House of Commons.

subtopic: JOSEPH DELPHIS GUILLAUME DELORME
speechtext: What about the petitioner? My hon. friend has told us of his attitude toward divorce.

subtopic: JOSEPH DELPHIS GUILLAUME DELORME

I know my hon. friend
believes in simply rubber stamping whatever the Senate has done. I do not believe in that.

subtopic: JOSEPH DELPHIS GUILLAUME DELORME
speechtext: You know better than that.

subtopic: JOSEPH DELPHIS GUILLAUME DELORME
speechtext: My hon. friend has illustrated a prejudiced type of mind in the discussion of this thing ever since this particular case came up, and I do not want to elaborate upon it, but I can if necessary. In the meantime, we have the hon. member's name recorded-I refer to the private members' bills-and in that connection he did vote "yea" that all these ten divorce bills be considered in that way without even reading the numbers and the names.

subtopic: JOSEPH DELPHIS GUILLAUME DELORME
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, on a question of privilege; that is absolutely untrue. I seconded the motion that they be dealt with individually. I do not want my hon. friend speaking for me in this house. If I want to make a speech in this house I will make my own speech.

subtopic: JOSEPH DELPHIS GUILLAUME DELORME
speechtext: I apologize unreservedly to the hon. gentleman. For a moment I was excited.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subtopic: JOSEPH DELPHIS GUILLAUME DELORME
speechtext:
Order. As soon as I sit down the hon. member for Saskatoon may continue his remarks. We may regard the incident between himself and the hon. member for Wellington South concluded. In the debate on clause 1 of the bill which is before us there may be, the committee will agree, no practical advantage in the chairman at the moment becoming too particular as to adherence to the rules. The only thing is that every time the rules are not adhered to the occasion becomes a precedent for another, and I think it is my duty to point out to the hon. member for Saskatoon that the over-all procedure on divorce bills is not before the committee at the moment. He has unlimited rights to debate the merits or


demerits of clause 1 of this bill, and clause 1 is the bill. But we are less likely to have a repetition of the unfortunate incident that almost occurred if we stick to the matter before the committee instead of endeavouring at this late stage to debate a very debatable question, namely, the manner of handling divorce cases as a whole, which might have been in order on the second reading but which, my hon. friend will agree, is not before the committee at the moment.

subtopic: JOSEPH DELPHIS GUILLAUME DELORME
speechtext:
Will you give me at least this much indulgence? Will you let me make my apologies to my hon. friend? Perhaps I was a trifle moved at the moment, and I made an error when I said that my hon. friend was one of those who asked that the bills be taken en masse on that particular occasion. I was totally and completely wrong. What I had meant to say was that he was recorded as being one of those who had voted in support of the preamble of this bill, which would have granted the divorce. Having said that, I cannot do anything else but again give him my humble apologies for having made that mistake. I hope I put myself in the clear in regard to the other matter at the same time.
This bill was considered a few days ago. It was considered on June 22, as will be found by referring to page 6482 of Hansard. In case any of my hon. friends wish to refer to that particular page, I want to warn them that there were a good many copies of yesterday's Hansard from which a number of pages were left out. When I went to refer to what I had said on the last day I could not find a part of my speech. The Hansard pages from 6467 to 6482 inclusive were missing in my copy. I then went to borrow the copy of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, and I found that the same thing had happened there. Finally, I did obtain a correct copy. I expect it happened to only one run of print. I found on page 6475 what the Secretary of State, who has interjected in this debate with an appeal of something or other, said on that occasion, and I shall try to answer him. He said:
Does this procedure have to be inflicted on the whole house?
I say yes, by the machinery which is set up for handling this matter, and I am most sorry to say that it does. The whole question, sir, is most distasteful to me and I must say that I am almost certainly not in character when I have to do this sort of thing.
Then I want to say a word in regard to the debate which took place in this house and I refer in particular to the hon. member

lor Charlevoix and his remarks as reported at page 6482 of Hansard where he is reported as having said:
After listening to all these complaints about these bills and listening to all this talk I am just wondering whether these hon. members who are complaining about these bills find their conscience bothered enough to rise and vote against the bills.
To that query, sir, and it is a legitimate one, my answer is yes. My conscience bothers me sufficiently so that I shall vote against this bill if the opportunity arises. I shall vote against any divorce bill in this house if in my own mind that decision is justified. What does one base one's decision upon? Well, he must base it, I suppose, on the evidence. I had hoped, sir, that there would be enough latitude given me to talk a little around this thing, but I have a very good copy of the evidence here if the house insists that I inflict it upon them, and I can quote from the evidence at some length. However, I am still hoping that will not be necessary, particularly in regard to the details and in regard to certain names.
I find that Bill No. 434 is of such a nature that I am compelled to vote against it. I find that according to the record of the miscellaneous private bills committee the preamble of this bill was opposed on a vote by six members of that committee. I propose to tell the committee who those six members were:	The hon. members for Regina City,
Lapointe, Macleod, Saskatoon, Mackenzie, and Burnaby-Coquitlam. I would like to say to the hon. member for Charlevoix, who is not here at the moment, and with whom I am not very well acquainted, that I imagine that with his background and training I expect he would be opposed to the whole idea of divorce in general upon moral and religious grounds, and I am going to suggest to him that if he go out behind the curtains and go up to the offices and gather in people of like mind and bring them into this house he could kill every divorce that came before this house at any time. I am not suggesting he should do that, but I am telling him he could do that if he so desires. Why does he not do that?
Why do they absent themselves from these votes? Where are they today? Where will they be when this divorce bill is voted upon, if it is voted upon today? I venture to say that there will be a smaller proportion in this house when the vote comes up than there was in the miscellaneous private bills committee of which I speak.
So, sir, on this matter of conscience let me turn the challenge back upon him. If it is a matter of conscience that he should oppose divorce bills then he should oppose them.
Private Bill-Divorce
If it is a matter of conscience for me to oppose this bill today then I am going to oppose it.
I do not expect my hon. friend has organized any group to come in here and kill this bill on conscientious grounds. If they are here I do not see them. As a matter of fact, sir, I do not see any hon. member on the government side of this house who is recorded as having done anything but vote for this particular divorce bill and so I propose to read to you the names of those who supported the preamble in the committee and by so doing recorded themselves as being in favour of this particular divorce.
The vote on the preamble is recorded and this is the vote on which I was unfortunate enough to blame my hon. friend. Those who voted for it were as follows: The hon. members for Timmins, Victoria-and I hope I have got them right for I do not want someone else jumping on my back-Wellington South, Parkdale, Jacques Cartier-Lasalle, Cumberland, the junior member for Queens, and Papineau. It is interesting to note that the latter was the gentleman who went on that committee instead of the hon. member for Laurier who had resigned and that the substitute also voted for that divorce. Then I have the hon. members for Lisgar, Manitoba; Middlesex East; and Selkirk. That is the record, and now the committee has the names of those who voted for and against this particular divorce from both sides of the house.
Just in case you think that was a small committee I want to point out, perhaps in justice to those concerned, that three members abstained from voting. They were the hon. members for High Park, Niagara Falls, and Wetaskiwin. That is the total number of the committee and this will show just how interested those men are in their work, and do not think I am blaming them for not being interested. There are 50 on that committee and the number present when that vote was taken was 20, three of whom abstained.
That is something of the history of this particular bill. I am still avoiding the evidence but I will come to it because I am going to try to show this house that this woman had a case equally as good perhaps against her husband. It happens in many cases that the men have the advantage in this thing, and I think that is probably chiefly true in the two provinces concerned, for there the man is the money earner and in many cases the keeper of the purse. The man probably has more know-how in legal matters and it is pretty hard for a woman

Private Bill-Divorce
in certain circumstances to set out with $1,500 in cash to start with, then the counsel's fees, and then find the money to pay these Peeping Tom investigators while they are engaged in their business, if we can call it business. The man can initiate that sort of thing and he sometimes gets away with it.
Now I want to say another word about this bill which originated, as so many of these bills do, in the province of Quebec. Some of them originated in the province of Newfoundland and I need not go into the history of why we get divorce cases from these two provinces. But I want to say that I deplore, whether in these two provinces, my own province, or any other province, the increase in the number of divorce cases, for it is a lamentable and pitiable thing, and the effect is that at this session of parliament we have had probably the greatest number of divorce cases, though the margin is small, than have ever been presented before at any one session of the Canadian House of Commons, certainly as far back as I think 1943 or 1947, and on a ten-year basis. I think it is on a ten-year basis. If any one of my hon. friends would like to get a record of that, I would commend them to the Senate committee report on divorce. It is No. 55. It is the minutes of proceedings of the Senate committee of Canada. It was issued on May 12, 1954. It will show them statistics there on divorce generally which I think they will find interesting to read.
I may say that this bill is one of 382 bills which were initiated from the provinces of Quebec and Newfoundland in this session. I see that the number from Newfoundland was 9, so it will not be hard for you to do the necessary mathematics and discover how many were initiated in the province of Quebec.

subtopic: JOSEPH DELPHIS GUILLAUME DELORME
speechtext: I think that with some co-operation from the hon. member who now has the floor we might keep this discussion away from the method of the handling of divorces as a whole, which is an extremely large subject. I do not think that I can rule the hon. member for Saskatoon out of order in relating this particular incident to one of a series of incidents and perhaps proving that they are on the increase or on the decrease. subtopic: JOSEPH DELPHIS GUILLAUME DELORME
speechtext:
I want to say that I think I was in order because I was discussing this bill. As a matter of fact, I was saying "this bill" when the hon. member interrupted me. I was just talking about this bill. I was saying that this bill originated from the province of Quebec where these matters are not dealt with in the same fashion as they are dealt with in other provinces. Our committee-and I am talking about the miscellaneous private bills committee which considered this bill-consisted of men, the great majority of whom were not from the province of Quebec or from the province of Newfoundland. I am submitting that it is quite a great responsibility for us, who have different arrangements with regard to divorce in our provinces, to take total responsibility or almost total responsibility for having to deal with cases which come from other provinces. I definitely feel that this case and cases like it should be more in the hands of the people of the provinces in which they originate than in those of people who come from provinces which have other arrangements with regard to these matters.

It is the right of Quebec, as it is the right of Newfoundland, to handle their own marriage problems in their own way. -and my friends will excuse me if I leave the girl's name out.

I want to come now to the main charge of this man that his wife had committed adultery. He tells us that nineteen years ago was the first time he knew of the adultery of his wife. He had come home at an unexpected time and had found his wife occupying sleeping quarters with another man. He said that he had found that also upon another occasion. So his counsel said: "What did you do?" He said, "I went out and cried." They asked him, "Did you wake them up?" He said, "I did not." On another occasion he said, "I went off to the hockey game and I cried." For nineteen years that man said he knew that she had been living in adultery with another man. When he found out about it he went out and cried, but he lived and cohabited with her for the next nineteen years, although he had said in his petition that he had by no means condoned the adultery of which she was accused.
I ask you: Why did he only now bring this petition of divorce against his wife? Well, the home was broken up. Why did he not bring suit immediately he discovered these things? Oh, he said, on account of the children. But nineteen years later when his wife, whom he had deserted in the meantime, brought a case in the Quebec courts for a separation which the petitioner allowed to go by default, and when my friend'-I must not call him that-when the petitioner discovered he had to pay $20 a week and was liable to have to do so for the rest of his life, he suddenly decided that this wife of his was a bad woman and that somehow or other he would have to get rid of her. page 12. The petitioner was being questioned by Mr. Lefrancois, his counsel. This is the

A. Well, it is then that I decided to do something.

Let us examine this question of the children for whom he showed such consideration, the little children who of course could not be disgraced by the stigma that would be attached to them. Who are these children' There are two boys. One is now eighteen and is unmarried and the other is twenty. They were before the committee. They were on the witness stand. The petitioner was asked where his children lived. He did not know where either of them lived. He was asked about his friendship with his children, and he said
that the last time he saw one of them_________I
have forgotten which one-he called him a name in French so dirty that he could not bear to translate it into English in this committee.
Then they asked these children what they thought of their father. They said they had been beaten, kicked and abused by him and that they had to leave home. That is the man who could not sue this woman for a divorce on the ground of adultery to which he swore because the children's name had to be protected. What a farce! On the stand that woman said that she knew her husband had been unfaithful to her. This is one instance where the case might just as well have been reversed with equal justice. It so happened that it was the petitioner who sued her and not she him.
I could go on. I have a lot of other evidence.
I saw the whole proceeding. On the one side there was the mother with her family. On the other side were the professional investigators, the principal one of whom admitted that he had received a small bonus of $20 oyer and above his fee for having come home with the bacon. I ask you: Are you going to believe that woman's son, that fine young boy in Her Majesty's air force uniform? Counsel tried to attack his character in committee and I refused to permit that. This man's wife left him and went to live in another house with a man who happened to be a cousin, a Mr. Delorme, a man with the same name. I have no disagreement at all with the evidence that has been presented. Remember this, and I say it sincerely, I have no more grief for the husband than I have for the wife. They were both the same.
