AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at seven o'clock.

When the committee rose at five o'clock to consider private bills I was making a few remarks on the Saskatchewan dam. I said at that time there was a considerable area of agreement between the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre and myself regarding his statement that the dam was approved of by all members in Saskatchewan. Later in his remarks, when describing the conditions in the 1930's when we had the dried-out period in the west, he said that when he drove down a street in Moose Jaw he was unable to see the engine of his car. Hon. members may have thought he had had a slip of the tongue, but what he was actually describing was the dust condition. We are not able to see the engines of our cars today, but there are hoods over them and they are largely ornamented with chrome. But in those days he was likely in the same condition as most residents of Saskatchewan. If they owned an automobile at that time the hood had long since blown away or had been used to repair the barn or to put a roof on some utilitarian building in the backyard.
That was the condition that existed at that time. What the hon. member was describing was that the dust conditions were so bad that as he drove down the street no doubt he had no hood on his car and he could not see the motor, not because there was a hood there but because of the dust. These were desperate days, and we do not want to see a recurrence. That is something we have no control over. Conservation of water is something over which we have some control. I agree with the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre when he says that all members from Saskatchewan are favourable to this dam. In this respect I am different from most members from Saskatchewan in that in my own constituency we have lots of water. As a matter of fact, in the Meadow Lake area we could fill this dam perhaps 150 times or 200 times over without any difficulty. We do realize that when other parts of the country are prosperous it makes a lot of difference to us as well.

I am in agreement with the hon. member tor Saskatoon who said that when this project is shown to be something that will benefit the nation as a whole it should be gone ahead with. This is about all I have to say at this time. I just want to indicate that I too am in agreement with the construction of the dam. When it is a national project, when we know that it is something that will benefit the nation as a whole, we should go ahead with it.

If or when this project is undertaken some of its store of water will be passing through the river Qu'Appelle, which is the northern boundary of the constituency I represent. Therefore, I hope the committee will forgive me for taxing its patience for about two minutes at this time. There are only two points I want to emphasize because I think the matter has been very thoroughly covered, particularly by the hon. member for Rosthern this afternoon. 1 endorse wholeheartedly the appeal he made to people from all parts of Canada and to members from all parts of Canada who represent constituencies in this house. To my mind the final decision to build this project will be made when members from other parts of Canada decide that it is in the national interest so to do.
The area in question has been under discussion for a long time. In fact we read of discussions having taken place or interest shown in the area where this dam would be constructed as far back as 150 years ago. In 1804, John McDonald of Garth, who represented the North West Company in western Canada, gathered a great deal of Indian legend concerning this area where at certain times at high flood the river would reverse its course. That is the area at the bend of the South Saskatchewan, and not so many miles from there are the headwaters of the Qu'Appelle river. So much interest was created at that time by those reports that various expeditions were organized to investigate the possibilities.
In fact waterways in western Canada is a subject that has been discussed internationally as far back as 1822 when there was a meeting between representatives of the United States and of Canada to discuss the feasibility of developing a waterway which would connect the great lakes and the Red river valley. Nothing much came of that, but there was a certain amount of interest and in July, 1859 a steamship by the name of "Anson" arrived at Fort Garry. Interest was again aroused and the Canadian government sent an expedition from eastern Canada headed by Henry Hind, professor of
Supply-Agriculture
geology of Trinity College, Toronto, called the Assiniboine and Saskatchewan exploring expedition. Hind had the vision of creating a waterway which would make it possible to travel by water from Fort Garry, now Winnipeg, right through along the Assiniboine, the Qu'Appelle, the Saskatchewan and the Bow river to the foothills of the Rockies. It is worth while mentioning the interest evidenced by the British government in this area when they sent out Captain Palliser in 1858.
I mention these few skimpy historical facts for this purpose and this purpose alone, namely, to show that the waterways of the western plains had been considered of national and also international interest long before 1954. I believe the interest was first aroused by the old Indian legends conveyed to the white people about 1804 when John McDonald made his explorations for the North West Company while trading with the Indians. I set forth these few historical facts because I believe that when the government and parliament makes its decision it could be helpful to be fully aware of the historical background of the project.
I am not going to cover the points raised by other hon. members, particularly the hon. member for Rosthern, but I want to stress another more practical point in particular. If this dam is constructed in the area I have mentioned it will constitute the main source of water supply for a large percentage of the people of Saskatchewan. The people in the city of Regina, some 75,000 in number, and the people in the city of Moose Jaw, the third largest city in Saskatchewan, will be assisted in obtaining a better water supply if the dam is built. Let me point out, in addition, that at the present time, as most hon. members know, there is a project by which water is going to be led from Buffalo Pound lake through to the city of Regina by pipe line. Buffalo Pound lake is the headwaters of the Qu'Appelle river.
It is desirable in all our water supplies to have the water pure, tasty, and as high a quality as possible. If we have a diversion of the South Saskatchewan by virtue of such a project as the South Saskatchewan dam then the water will be flowing through Buffalo Pound lake until it finally finds its way into the Qu'Appelle river and then on down to Manitoba. In order to keep the water as pure as possible it is desirable to have a steady flow from the headwaters, but in this case the headwaters are not of sufficient flow to provide the required degree of freshness in that water and it would have to be treated. I am not saying it is not pure at the present time because Moose Jaw

Supply-Agriculture
is using this water. It would be desirable to have a larger volume of water available so that the quality would be considerably improved. This project when completed will accomplish this.
Let me remind members of the committee that this will be a very large structure. If the people of Canada decide to undertake this project then we will be creating a lake about two-thirds the length of lake Erie. I do not think many people allow their imagination to dwell on the fact that in the heart of one of the finest agricultural areas of this country we will be providing a lake of such magnitude. Apart from irrigation and power requirements more than 100,000 people in the heart of Saskatchewan are depending on this project for better and purer drinking water. I would like to add my voice to that of those who have already spoken on this subject and I would like to urge all members of the house to consider both the background, the necessity, and the economic value to the Canadian people as a whole and particularly in the area, of this project. It will help the people of Saskatchewan to a better life personally and in making a living. It will increase the natural growth, strength, and the virility of the Dominion of Canada.

49. Maritime Marshland Rehabilitation Act $2,097,180.	1

Mr. Chairman, after all the dry talk from the west, perhaps we can come down to the maritimes where the maritime marshland rehabilitation activities are somewhat comparable to prairie farm rehabilitation. I am sure that any observer in the gallery of the house during this session would come to the conclusion that the only place in Canada where any agriculture is carried on is the western provinces. If my figures are right, one-third of those in Canada who make their living off the land reside in the three western provinces and, important though it is to the income of this country, they produce little more than two-fifths of the cash income from farms. Therefore I do believe that agriculture in the rest of Canada should receive some attention.
I come now to the question of maritime marshland rehabilitation. This project, as I said a moment ago, is comparable to what is going on in the west. At the outset I should like to say how pleased we in the maritime provinces are that this great work has been undertaken. We have a splendid force of men working there and they are doing a good job. It is true that when they first came to the area a great many of them were in the position of dealing with something new. They were used to having one or two floods a year to control. In the regions adjoining the bay of Fundy there are four floods a day to look after. The tide goes out twice a day and comes in twice a day and each tide, whether in or out, is a rush of water. As a matter of fact at Burntcoat in my constituency we have the highest tides in the world. The difference between high tide and low tide is 62 feet.
That is the kind of situation these engineers found themselves confronted with when they started to rehabilitate our marshlands. Sometimes I wonder just what manner of men the old Acadians were who won these lands back from the sea. They had no engineering staff. They were their own engineers. For tools they had a spade, an axe and probably a plow. For power they had a team of oxen. Yet they built the works, reclaimed the lands,

Supp ly-A griculture
and the works have stood the test for centuries. I only hope that in our present day and generation our men are building as well as the people of old.
Now, I might speak of this Maritime Marshland Rehabilitation Act. It was my privilege, in the former days when I was a member of this house, to be somewhat interested in this project. I recall very well that we carried the ball on that item between 1936 and 1945. We had the subject before the committee on rehabilitation, and they recommended it. Then, we took it up with the Minister of Agriculture and with the ministers of agriculture of the three maritime provinces. The provincial ministers looked upon it as an entirely federal project. After some discussion it was decided that those of us who were very much interested in this project should perhaps take a little more active part, so there was an unofficial committee formed. This unofficial committee conferred on the problem with the Minister of Agriculture and the various provincial ministers of agriculture. The committee consisted of the hon. member for Westmorland, then Mr. Emmerson; the then member for Queens, Prince Edward Island, Mr. Douglas, and myself. Unfortunately, the two first-named gentlemen have now gone to their great reward, so it remains for me, as the last remaining member of the committee, to perhaps reminisce for one moment.
As I say, we went to work and we eventually persuaded the provincial ministers of agriculture that they should also participate in this great project. Eventually it was worked out as a three-way plan, with the federal government keeping the water off the land; the provincial government arranging for the larger drainage canals, and the land owners looking after the small drainage canals. As I said a moment ago, we worked on this project for years. It was my great pleasure, before my services were dispensed with for a time by the electors of Colchester -Hants, to find in the estimates a small amount for general surveys and for a little exploratory work. I am happy today to see that the infant I left here in 1945 has now grown to a very commendable size. As a matter of fact the expenditure on the project, including this year, has been something in the neighbourhood of $8 million or $9 million, along with considerable provincial money and the land owners' contributions.
Now, with that background I was probably a little bit prejudiced but rather interested the other day to hear the Leader of the Opposition claim that the Bennett administration was responsible for the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act; that may be so. Possibly they are responsible to the same extent

the Rhodes-Harrington government in Nova Scotia was responsible for old age pensions. They passed such an act, and then never did anything about it. It is peculiar how the Conservatives try to take credit for these things. I recall being in the local house at the time this legislation was enacted, and I had something to do with the provincial government legislation which is complementary to this act. I recall that in the federal parliament the then member for Colchester -Hants said that the Minister of Agriculture was entitled to some credit for putting in this act but that the member for Cumberland, Mr. Black, was entitled to most of the credit. When I recall some of the things that happened from 1935 to 1945, I can say that it is true Mr. Black did make two or three speeches in the house. However, I know from experience that with a project like this you have to do more work than speak in the house.
However, this great project is continuing and there are now 119 marsh bodies under this reclamation scheme in the maritimes. They have reclaimed some 66,000 acres and along with this there are 375,000 acres of land being operated. Perhaps that is not a large area in the grain growing country, but in the maritimes it is quite a lot of land. Again I wish to compliment the engineers and the director of this work for what they are doing. There is just one other thought I am going to leave with them. Their work is not yet completed. Let them carry on, and complete the work.
There is another problem in the maritimes, and that is our meadow lands and our interval lands. When our marshlands are reclaimed this commission should, during the interval, be studying what could be done to save the interval lands because year by year they are going to the sea. Unless we can keep a good percentage of our people in Nova Scotia gainfully employed on the land we will not be able to take our full part in this great dominion as our forefathers intended we should do. As I say, if the engineers in the maritime field could study the problem along our various river valleys-such great rivers as the Stewiacke, Musquodoboit, North Salmon and St. Mary's-they will find there are large areas going to sea. After it goes to sea, it is no good. If we could keep these areas in production in Nova Scotia, it would maintain this beauty spot and this great asset to Canada.

To provide, subject to the approval of the governor in council, for assistance to farmers in Manitoba and Saskatchewan for crop losses that occurred between the 1st day of August, 1950, and the 14th day of May, 1953, in respect of which there is no authority under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act to make awards.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Like the hon. member for Brant-Haldimand I found it difficult to understand this vote. I believe it would be well if I were to place the explanation on record that is given with respect to it.
The Prairie Farm Assistance Act, paragraph (c), subsection 3 of section 3, was amended in 1950 to provide, inter alia, that crown and municipal lands not sold or granted prior to December 31, 1940, would not be eligible for award. An amendment in 1951 excluded from the provisions of the 1950 amendment all lands lying north of the south boundary of township sixty in the provinces of Alberta and British Columbia. A further amendment in 1953 excluded from the provisions of the 1950 amendment other lands in the northern parts of Manitoba and Saskatchewan.
The amendment of 1951 with respect to the lands in Alberta and British Columbia came into force on August 1, 1950, while the 1953 amendment with respect to the Manitoba and Saskatchewan lands became effective on May 14, 1953.
The situation is the same in all four provinces with respect to the lands affected by these amendments, and the advisability of making the effective dates the same has been recommended because a number of farmers in Manitoba and Saskatchewan excluded from award by the 1950 amendment suffered
IMr. Pickersgill.]
crop losses prior to 1953 and it is felt that they are as entitled to awards as the farmers in Alberta. However, the number of such farmers and the amount involved is so small, being no more than $17,000, it is recommended instead that an ex gratia payment be made to such farmers.
According to a Department of Justice opinion, such ex gratia payments can be made to these farmers upon executive approval, but it would be necessary to have a special item in the supplementary estimates to which the payments would be charged.

The substance of the remarks of the parliamentary assistant, as I understand it, is that this was contrary to legislation passed by parliament, and this estimate is now brought forward to be approved by parliament in another form.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: That is right.
And I suppose the minister justifies it on the basis of some equities that make it proper. But the fact remains that we are undoing what parliament has already done.
My understanding is that this is to bring it into line with farmers in other provinces.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

It is to put the farmers of Saskatchewan on the same basis as farmers m British Columbia and Alberta, who were treated that way under the amendment. If that is what it is, then there is no objection to it. But I must say that it struck me in the same way as it did my hon. friend, that unless there is a question of equity involved and this removes the unfairness, there could be no excuse for it. Then, the amount is small, and that struck me rather forcibly, because I would have thought there would have been many more farmers entitled to this than apparently there are, according to this vote.

However attractive it may be to have people altering the law in order to produce what they consider to be equity, it is rather a far-reaching conception, if they are prepared to accept it. We might have different ideas of what equities are. It often happens even among such reasonable men as ourselves. One really wonders how far it is going to go. The question of legislation by estimate has been up here before, and I think the Prime Minister went on record as frowning on it very severely.

This may be the one exception that should be tolerated. It seems to me a very questionable procedure.

It is obvious we cannot inquire into the equities of the cases here tonight. If the minister would table a list of cases and the payments made to these people, then any hon. member who is interested in inquiring could see it. That would probably meet the situation.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: The only reason I intervene in this is that I am a member of the government and I was present when the decision was made to ask the committee to pass this estimate. No payments have yet been made because the government had no authority to make any payment. We are now humbly asking this committee to allow us to make the payments. The argument that was put before us, and which convinced us that we should ask for this, was that in 1950 certain townships up to a certain distance north-I cannot remember the parallel of latitude-were included under the act in British Columbia and Alberta. Saskatchewan and Manitoba were not included because there were practically no farming areas that far north in Saskatchewan and Manitoba. It was subsequently discovered that there were a few areas in the northern parts of Saskatchewan and Manitoba which should be included, and we in the government felt that what parliament thought was good for Alberta and British Columbia, parliament would think was good for Manitoba and Saskatchewan. It so happened that parliament had brought Manitoba and Saskatchewan under the act last year, but it was found there were a few cases of hardship in the intervening period between those two dates, and it was thought that to amend the whole act for this purpose would really not be warranted; that this was the kind of thing that could properly be provided for in the estimates. That is the explanation, and that is why we are asking authority to make these payments.

By the same token, if an individual in Ontario, for instance, had a complete crop failure he would be as much entitled to this as anyone else. It is outside the area, and the government is starting a precedent, and you might have demands from many sections.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
As it was explained to us, these payments are governed by the same rules precisely as are applied under the act.

In general for a few moments tonight I should like to deal with some of the publications issued by the fisheries research board which are included in these estimates. I asked a question about this matter on the orders of the day some time ago. The Minister of Fisheries apparently did not read the question. He read the newspaper reports thereon, and he replied at some length in the house a while ago. At that time the minister claimed that the purpose of these publications was to exchange information between scientists in Canada and elsewhere, and with that we can have very little quarrel. Referring to these publications, the minister said that it is really a measure of economy avoiding waste by duplication of effort just through the limited publication of current investigations.
The interesting thing about that is that according to the return tabled in the house by the Secretary of State in answer to my question none of these publications has ever been sold, not one copy, and not one copy has been distributed without charge. In other words, according to the parliamentary return tabled in the house, the printing of these publications has served absolutely no useful purpose. They have been printed and they have not been distributed. The parliamentary return is sessional paper No. 117-A, tabled on Wednesday, April 7, 1954.
The minister in the course of his remarks did make one rather interesting assertion. In order to demonstrate the small cost to the taxpayer, as the minister saw it, of these various publications he argued that the wastage which he admitted can be calculated by taking the remaining copies which are on hand and valuing them at their selling price. The resulting figure according to him represents the waste arising from the printing of the publications. I am going to explore this a litle bit because it smacks very much of the same kind of financial wizardry which

we were discussing a few minutes ago in connection with travelling expenses. The minister said, as found at page 4506 of Hansard of May 7:
The important point as far as waste is concerned is the amount which is surplus.
As an example of his mathematics, he referred to the publication covering the cruising speed of goldfish. You will remember that one. There was another one on "Abdominal Width and Sexual Maturity of Female Lobsters on the Canadian Atlantic Coast", commonly referred to by most of the newspapers as "The sex life of the lobster". With reference to the one on the cruising speed of goldfish the minister said:
We have thirteen copies of this left at 20 cents each, which means a surplus cost of $2.60.
The argument that the selling price and not the cost of the publication determines the cost of the service to the taxpayer is completely misleading, unethical and fallacious. It is like saying that the fire department of a city does not cost the municipal taxpayer a cent because he does not have to foot the bill when he calls the fire department to put out a fire. If you used this argument in the way it is used by the minister you could print a million copies of a publication for free distribution, then decide not to distribute them, and there would be no wastage because even as thirteen times 20 cents is $2.60-and he says that is the surplus cost in that case-a million times zero is still zero.
Therefore according to his argument a million copies of a publication which he has printed and then decided to throw away have not cost the taxpayer a cent. Obviously too this sort of argument means that the more valuable a publication becomes in so far as its selling price is concerned, the more the taxpayer is saved by the government giving it away. This curious type of saving increases steadily as more and more copies are given away for nothing.
For example, if the government has on hand 1,000 copies of a $2 publication, the wastage according to the minister's reasoning is $2,000. If they give away 500 copies, the wastage drops to only $1,000. If they give them all away, then there is no wastage at all. I am using the minister's reasoning and everything except the minister's figures. Pursuing this argument to its logical conclusion, and using the minister's reasoning exactly as he used it-it must be good reasoning because he is a Rhodes scholar, Mr. Chairman; if this is the type of reasoning that comes from Rhodes scholars on the government side, I am glad we have a different type of Rhodes scholar on our side.

So are we.

In pursuing this Rhodes scholar type of reasoning, there would be absolutely no wastage at all if, as soon as these publications were received from the printer, they were all dumped into the Ottawa river. Perhaps that is what the minister had in mind when he developed his arguments. In any event, I shudder to think what might happen if some of the rumours we have heard recently become true and the Minister of Fisheries becomes the Minister of Finance, and retains his philosophy that the more you throw away the more you save. It practically qualifies him to lead the Social Credit party.
Louder and funnier.

A few days ago the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings told a very interesting little story in the house. As I remember it was about a fish ladder built in his constituency, only when the ladder was built there was not any water so they had to go around and bail the fish out, then dump them above the ladder. This sounds amusing at first. It is hard to believe that any sensible, sane, sound group of men would do things like that.
But let us have another example, stating facts again, to see what these hon. gentlemen from the other side can do. In his attempt to defend some of these publications, you will remember the publications which the parliamentary return said had not been sold or given away, one of them concerned the cruising speed of goldfish. The minister said it resulted from research in connection with the Hell's Gate fishway in the Fraser river canyon. He said these were fish studies carried out in order to determine the range and cruising speed of fish. Then he went on to say how valuable that information was in connection with fisheries.
The truth of the matter is, Mr. Chairman, that according to the international Pacific salmon fisheries commission, bulletin 3, page 10, the right bank of the fishway was completed in the spring of 1945. The left bank fishway was constructed in two sections; the lower end was completed in the spring of 1945 and the upper section was not finished until the spring of 1946. In other words, everything was done by the spring of 1946. The pamphlet referred to was received for publication in March, 1947, covering experiments carried out between October 25 and November 30, 1946. This is an interesting fact, because it shows just how the taxpayer's money can be spent, and the government attitude towards so many of these things. It is apparent that, having completed

Supply-Fisheries
in the spring of 1946 the new fishways at an approximate cost of $2 million, about six months later in the fall of 1946 the government commenced an experiment with goldfish to see whether the fishways would work.
I think, Mr. Chairman, in all sincerity that we can stand here and be glad that despite such bungling the fishways do work and that they are doing a job for the fisheries on the Pacific coast. Certainly it is no thanks to the government who built them first, then tried to find out later whether or not they worked.
Undoubtedly we are going to hear from one or two hon. members before very long who will try to turn these words of mine, as the Minister of Fisheries did previously; try to turn them into some sort of indictment of fisheries research generally. They will try to infer from these words that I am opposed to constructive undertakings in this field. I suppose that is part of debate, taking sincere words of a member on this side of the house and trying to controvert them or twist them and make them mean something else.
I want to make it clear, Mr. Chairman, to all those who may read or hear these remarks, that honest publication of worth-while things which are needed and used by people or by scientists is a good thing. I want to make it quite plain that, in my estimation at least, and I think that of my colleagues, good research, purposeful research, sincere and intelligent research is something that has the wholehearted approbation of myself and my colleagues.
But, Mr. Chairman, that does not necessarily condone, and I do not condone, such things as research which is carried on after a project is completed in order to see whether it is going to work. It does not condone publication of research which nobody wants to read. It does not condone, in another field, the transfer of remuneration to people who may be doing this research from a branch in which it is taxable into a field in which it is not taxable. It does not condone the hiding of honoraria and other things like that, and including them in another category. It does not condone, Mr. Chairman-the government will be glad to hear this because we are coming to the end of the session and it is probably the last thing I will have to say this session; I am glad I can make this my closing remarks-for one moment the continuous wastage of public funds which could be more effectively spent in other ways, and the almost misrepresentation of this wastage and the attempt to make it sound as if it was doing a useful purpose.

The above are excerpts from government publications which are not available for free distribution_
That means free distribution by the printing bureau. In other words they are for sale, and they are in the catalogue if anybody wants to buy them. It appeared that nobody did want to buy them from the queen's printer; and I think it is perfectly obvious why nobody wanted to buy them from the queen's printer because, in spite of their titillating titles, I do not think they are very popular reading, and I doubt if even my hon. friend from Kamloops would be very worried about having them in the hands of children. They are provided by the department concerned-in this case the Department of Fisheries-for the use of technical staffs and for exchange purposes between scientists.
I said a little while ago that I did not know whether honoraria were taxable, because I never had received an honorarium. But, as hon. members know, I used to be an academic-while I was still respectable-and in that capacity I occasionally published articles in magazines. One could always get a number of extra copies of them for practically nothing, for about the cost of the paper. Putting the impression on a few extra copies, even by the Queen's Quarterly, which I am sure the hon. member for Greenwood would agree is not run extravagantly or wastefully, could be done at almost no extra cost.
That is why these extra prints are produced. And they are stuck in the catalogue- that is in the queen's printer's catalogue- just in case somebody somewhere might see them and want to buy one of them. And it is done in order to make this a complete catalogue of all government publications.
I have made it my business to know a little about what the fisheries research board is doing, because it concerns the livelihood of most of the people who voted for me, and most of the people who voted against me

in the last election. And I doubt if there is any organization in the whole of the government service that is doing better work. I do not say there are not many others that are doing just as good work, but I do not think they are doing better work than is being done by this board. And I am sure the papers they publish are things that are worth having some permanent record of. I do not pretend to be a scientist and I am not going to pretend that I can say precisely what they are worth.
Then, on the other point raised by the hon. member, while I am no expert on the income tax, I am told that whether an allowance is called an honorarium or a per diem allowance, the income tax branch takes exactly the same view of it.

On May 7 I asked the minister about the situation in Hecate strait so far as the crab fisheries are concerned. At that time he promised to bring in some figures. I should like to point out to the parliamentary assistant that this situation appears to be very serious, namely, that American fishing vessels are getting the great bulk of the crabs being caught in Hecate strait. They are taking them up to an American fishing port in Alaska, and apparently are doing a big business. Canadians are worried for fear the whole fisheries will be ruined before something is done by the government.
I have here a copy of a publication known as the Pacific Fisherman. This is the issue of August, 1953. In it I find an interesting article with the heading "Pacific Pearl of Alaska". Pacific Pearl is the name of an American company. Then there is a subheading which states "New Industry is built upon Hecate Strait Crab Resource". Reading the first paragraph, I find this:
Four years have made Ketchikan, Alaska, the principal center of Pacific crab canning-four years and one company-Pacific Pearl of Alaska, Inc., which initiated the operation there in 1950.
Then the article goes on to say:
Two developments took Pacific Pearl to Alaska:
First, the cyclic shortage of crabs on the Washington coast, where the organization previously had centered its activities.
Second, the proving of a substantial population of Pacific crabs in the international waters of Dixon entrance and Hecate strait.
Dixon entrance is between the northern shore of the Queen Charlotte islands and Alaska; but Hecate strait lies between Queen Charlotte islands and the mainland of British Columbia. The article explains that there are eight of these boats carrying on the crab fisheries. It goes on to say:
These boats are able to carry around 1,200 dozen crabs each in a full load. All are equipped to use their holds as live tanks, supplied by pumps with
Supply-Fisheries
a constant supply of fresh sea-water . . . Each boat fishes from 400 to 500 crab pots-drum-shaped iron frames, protected from electrolysis by rubber coverings, and with the netting made of stainless steel wire.
Then we find the subheading "International Ocean Waters yield Prime Crab Catch". It shows clearly that the Americans regard Hecate strait as international waters in which they have as much right as Canadians. It says:
Fishing is done in international waters in Dixon entrance, through which passes the boundary line between Alaska and British Columbia; and in Hecate strait, separating the Queen Charlotte islands from the Canadian mainland ... In mid-summer at the latitude of Dixon entrance and Hecate strait the long hours of daylight permit the crab boats to find and haul their pots 21 hours out of the 24. Operations usually are suspended at midnight, to be resumed at 3 in the morning. Such hours mean hard work for the crew, and the job is anything but a rest. Once a boat has run her string, she heads for home-
That is, for Alaska.
-without a moment's waiting. Her hold is full of thousands of scuttling, clawing crabs, as lively and pugnacious as when they crawled and clashed on the sandy sea bed.
These crabs, which I claim are Canadian crabs, are taken to an Alaskan port and are shipped into the mainland of the United States as American crabs. They do not have to pay any duty. A Canadian fisherman who catches some of the crabs in the strait has to pay duty in order to sell those same crabs to the United States. The only place he has any protection at all is within three miles of the shore, and I believe that practically all the crab fishing is done beyond the three-mile limit.
I believe the crab fisheries off the Washington coast have been pretty well cleaned out, and I am afraid the same will happen in Hecate strait. We will wake up one of these days to find that while we have been trying to get up enough courage to tell the Americans that Hecate strait is Canadian territorial water, their fishermen will have cleaned out all the Canadian crabs. The parliamentary assistant must realize that that situation is intolerable. I hope he can give some reassurance tonight that the government is moving to put a stop to this procedure.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Fisheries
speechtext:
When the estimates were before the committee on May 7 the minister did promise to bring in certain information for the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra relative to crab fishing catches in Hecate strait.
Data concerning the catch of crabs by Americans in the year 1953 are not yet available. The only source from which we can get this information is Seattle, and it is not yet available to us for 1953. However we do

Supply-Fisheries
know that there were 19 crab fishing vessels all well equipped with the latest offshore pots and operating at that time in Hecate strait.
Is that 1953 or 1954?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Fisheries
speechtext:
As of June 20, 1953 there were 19 crab fishing vessels all equipped with live wells and the latest offshore pots. Of this number 10 were American, 8 from Washington state and two from California. These were using 5,100 crab pots. The remaining eight were Canadian vessels fishing 2,990 pots. The American fishery, however, in 1953 represented an increase of 2,500 traps over 1952. Then I can give the hon. member the statistics for the last three years. The American catch of crabs in Hecate strait: in 1950 they had six operating vessels and the catch was 880,292 pounds; in 1951 they had seven vessels operating and the catch was 960,749 pounds; in 1952 they had five vessels operating there and the catch was 1,169,062 pounds.
During the same period the landings of crabs taken by Canadian fishermen in the area of Hecate strait and Dixon entrance were for the year 1950, 722,000 pounds; in 1951, 808,303 pounds; in 1952,	1,105,100
pounds, and for 1953, 1,703,500 pounds.
Has the parliamentary assistant the figures for Hecate strait as distinguished from the other?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Fisheries
speechtext: No.
These are not the figures I asked for. I asked for the figures for Hecate strait. The parliamentary assistant has included the figures from Dixon entrance, which I was not questioning.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Fisheries
speechtext: The American figures I gave are for Hecate strait, purely for Hecate strait.
The figures for the Americans were only Hecate strait?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Fisheries
speechtext: Hecate strait.
What are the Canadian figures?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Fisheries
speechtext: I have not them broken down in that way. I am told that the statistical department has not broken them down in that way.

The Canadian figures are valueless if they include Hecate strait and Dixon entrance. Incidentally, the American figures are higher than the Canadian figures as it is except 1950, and the latter include both Hecate strait and Dixon entrance.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Fisheries
speechtext: That is the way the figures are kept in our breakdown. I regret I cannot give any other figures at this time.
I am told that as much as 80 per cent of the crabs taken from the three-mile limit in Hecate strait are taken by the Americans. Do the parliamentary assistant's officials quarrel with that estimate?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Fisheries
speechtext: The officials tell me they can neither confirm nor deny that statement. They have no means of knowing whether it is correct or not.
This fisheries research board has scientists on Queen Charlotte islands every summer. Is it not possible for them to find out what is happening there?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Fisheries
speechtext: It would be possible for our officials to break these statistics down as far as Canadian catches are concerned, but as far as American catches are concerned, we have to rely on figures furnished by the American officials.

Will the parliamentary assistant get those figures? He has given me the Canadian crab figures for the Dixon entrance and Hecate strait combined. He can have the Hecate strait figures sent to me during the recess.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Fisheries
speechtext:
I will endeavour to do that, Mr. Chairman. Whenever the figures are provided to me, I will see that they are forwarded to the hon. member.
In connection with the other matter he brought up, namely, the international aspect of the Hecate strait, this is a matter that has caused concern to the department for many years. At the present time, as the hon. gentleman knows, it is receiving the consideration of an interdepartmental committee. I do not know when a report will be available, but I know the matter is receiving active consideration.
No actual step has been taken since we discussed this matter in the house earlier in the session?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Fisheries
speechtext: No.
Has the Canadian government taken the stand that Hecate strait is Canadian territorial water?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I understand that our view has always been that it is territorial water, and the American view is that it is the open sea. The same thing applies of course on the east coast in a good many places. We have never been able to reconcile a good many of these differences. As the hon. member knows, there is a case before the international court at the present time which may codify the international law in this respect. But there is no very effective way in which we can force the Americans to accept our view.
In other words, there is no way in which we can stop the Americans from taking our crabs?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: We say they are ours; they say they are in the open sea.
You are not going to stop at that. Does the minister say that Canada is going to sit back because the Americans say this water is international water and there is nothing we can do about it?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I am sure the government would be delighted to have any practical suggestion that the hon. member for Van-couver-Quadra, or any other hon. member, could make as to how we can get the Americans to accept our view, as we certainly would like to have them accept our view.
Why not have the matter taken to the international court? Is there any objection to that?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I could not say, but I shall be glad to bring the suggestion to the attention of my colleagues.

He wanted to know whether any additions would be made to the St. Andrews biological station this year. I want to put on record the fact that the department is aware that the space available there for scientists is rather inadequate, and that every consideration is being given to the advisability of enlarging it.

The item which has just been passed, this item and the next two items cover substantially all of the research work of the Department of Fisheries, and includes the substantial amount of $2,500,000. The research which relates to great lakes fisheries, I take it, is carried on in conjunction with the research board with which I had some association in Ontario. I am interested to know the relationship between the federal fisheries research board and the inland fisheries research and whether its jurisdiction is nation-wide. If the parliamentary assistant can tell me that I should like to make one or two further comments.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Fisheries
speechtext:
The scope of the board is nation-wide; it covers all of Canada, since it is carrying on investigations in the inland waters as well as on the Pacific and the Atlantic coasts.
Supply-Fisheries

I take it the investigation in the great lakes is carried on in conjunction with provincial agencies, and that the whole thing is co-ordinated, as it ought to be. It is a very important and difficult kind of research, as I know. As every fisherman knows, the habits, the presence and the absence of fish, what makes them come and go, and where they are, is one of the most difficult things to deal with scientifically. The experiments on the great lakes that are helping to maintain these inland fisheries are of great importance, I assume, to people on both coasts and in all sections who make their livelihood from fishing.
The board with which I was concerned was the Ontario research board. It was made up of knowledgeable and reputable people who were good enough to lend their time and effort to direction of very substantial research expenditures. It is gratifying to know that there are people who will come forward for this kind of activity. I was interested to know the size of this board. I take it, it is distributed geographically, which is only fair. If the parliamentary assistant has no objection I am sure parliament would be glad to have the names of these people who are offering themselves voluntarily in this way to the furtherance of scientific research. If the names could be given to the committee so that we could recognize them for the work they are doing I would appreciate it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Fisheries
speechtext: I have not the names in front of me at the moment, but if this item could pass, one of the officials will write them up and then I can put them on the record in a few moments.

Mr. Chairman, I cannot
help but be interested in an item amounting to more than $107,000 for travelling expenses. I am just wondering whether the parliamentary assistant or the minister, who gave us such a delightful exposition in Twillingate in answer to my last question, would care to give us a breakdown.

The work of the biological stations, particularly, is spread over large areas

and the workers must cover those areas at intervals and for varying periods of time. This item makes provision for this necessary cost of the investigations. The terms approved for the employment of student assistants provide for the payment of transportation expenses, less $30, in reporting for duty and returning to home or university and this item provides for those costs. The provision of transportation to work of employees at the Atlantic biological station and the Pacific biological station is also included. The first item in the breakdown was $34,000?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Fisheries
speechtext: That is correct.
Exactly on whom was that spent?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Fisheries
speechtext: The directors and the senior staff.
How many people?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Fisheries
speechtext: It seems from the check of the statistics in front of me that about 125 persons are covered.
The fisheries research department then has 125 directors and senior staff. Is that a correct assumption from the parliamentary assistant's answer?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Fisheries
speechtext:
That is approximately
correct.

In other words we have here, Mr. Chairman, an organization whose staff appears to be composed entirely of generals with very few privates. That would seem to be the case for we have in the headquarters administration about 14 people_

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: We have 450 people there.

-and in the operation and maintenance staff we have some 442 including such persons as 73 seasonal assistants.
I am sure they are not included in the group, and I am quite sure assistant scientists would not be included.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Surely assistant scientists must be regarded as senior personnel. Look at the salaries.

I do not think we said "personnel". We said directors and senior staff. In other words, senior officials. I know it is a little bit annoying to the parliamentary assistant but we have seen cases in which we have had to watch the terminology being used in this house very carefully-

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: We certainly have.
In other words, one out of every three of the people involved in this scientific organization would appear to be senior members of the senior staff. Is that correct?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I wonder what else the hon. member would expect in a scientific organization which is engaged primarily in research. Would he expect a major number of the employees to be common labourers or office boys or would he expect them to be scientists?

147. To provide for federal share of administrative expenses of great lakes fisheries research committee established jointly with the province of Ontario; and to provide for a program designed to eliminate lampreys in the great lakes, $165,000.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to ask how the department is getting along with the elimination of the lampreys in the great lakes which play such havoc with white-fish and other fish. I am just asking that out of curiosity because I think we have heard about this every year and I would like to hear about it once more.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Fisheries
speechtext: Perhaps I could refer the hon. gentleman to an article which was published in the Trade News of May 1954 and if the hon. gentleman has not got a copy I will see that he gets one.
Thank you very much.

Mr. Chairman, I notice there has been a substantial increase in this item and I wonder if the parliamentary assistant could explain in what way the activities of this particular enterprise are going to be augmented.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Fisheries
speechtext: The federal government and the Ontario provincial government last year established a great lakes fisheries research committee to carry on and expand fisheries research in the Canadian waters of the great lakes, and various experiments are being carried out there, especially on lake Superior. Does the parliamentary assistant mean that because of the entry of the lampreys into lake Superior that the amount for the investigation has been trebled for this year?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Fisheries
speechtext:
Well, it is more than an investigation. Electrical devices are to be used to see if they will be effective in killing

the lampreys and they are also experimenting with certain types of poison. It has really got beyond the experimental stage now.

I am sure the parliamentary assistant will agree with me that it would arouse anyone's curiosity when the amount is trebled even if we were to admit that this money was being spent for a good purpose. But we would still like to have an explanation of the increase from $50,000 to $150,000 and we would like to know just what the department proposes to do.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I suppose the fact that the Ontario government is also willing to spend more on this project will reassure the hon. lady.
Is this a case of matching expenditure?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Fisheries
speechtext: Yes, the Ontario government pays an amount equal to that paid by the federal government.
That seems to me to be an extraordinary argument. For all we know the Ontario government may be using exactly the same argument to justify their item.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: They probably are.
Surely the minister can think of a better answer than that.
Could the parliamentary assistant give us an idea of how many personnel are involved in these experiments?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Fisheries

What I mean is this: If the federal government is putting up all this money, albeit that it is the Ontario government that is being assisted in the matter, surely we should have some idea as to how many persons are involved, what they are doing or how many lampreys are being killed.

seriously.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
I shall endeavour to give as serious an explanation as can possibly be

Supply-Fisheries
given of this item. I have never seen a lamprey. I am reminded by a very distinguished member of this committee that King John died of a surfeit of these animals. I hope the committee this evening is not going to suffer the same fate. As I understand it, the lamprey is an extremely serious pest in the great lakes where a large number of very worthy citizens of this province-and many of them in the county in which I happened to be born, Norfolk county-make their living. I understand that the Ontario government and the federal government became seriously concerned about this matter and that we were able to arrange some kind of co-operation with the Americans. I am not sure of what the details of this arrangement were; after all, this is not my department. I understand that we did reach an arrangement in co-operation with the Ontario government which, as hon. members know, administers the fisheries in that province, whereby we were to contribute 50 per cent of the cost of this scheme.
Perhaps this is not the right kind of political statement to make, but our experience in most of our dealings with the Ontario government has been that when they go into a project of this sort with us, they do so seriously and co-operate well. I am quite convinced that this is being done well. If there are any specific details that I cannot give or that the hon. member for St. Paul's cannot give-after all, he has had perhaps more to do with starting this project than anyone else in the committee-I shall be glad to make an effort to get them.

I should like to make one thing quite clear. I have in the past spent some time on commercial fishing boats on the great lakes; that is, on boats out of Port Dover in the riding from which the Secretary of State comes, his birthplace. I realize that this is a great problem and an important one. I have some firsthand personal knowledge of it. But despite the fact that I have no doubt or that, in fact, I have every confidence that everything the Ontario government does in this regard is excellent, nevertheless as a matter of principle I do not think it is exactly wise that the federal government-although with the best of intentions-should vote large sums of money like this without knowing exactly what they are for.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: To mention just a few figures about Indian affairs. Last year we built 972 new houses for the accommodation of Indians on reserves in accordance with our policy of continuing to build suitable housing every year. We have had a noteworthy increase in the attendance of Indian children at the schools, and the number as of March 31 was 31,555. This is an increase of 2,756 or nearly 10 per cent over last year, and the number of Indians now attending non-Indian schools stands at 3,381, an increase of 531 over the figure reported a year ago.

I wonder if the minister
could give a breakdown of the school children in their respective grades so that we may learn how many are at high school, and so on. The minister might give that breakdown later on.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Certainly. I could not leave the subject of education, Mr. Chairman, without mentioning a recent agreement we reached with the corporation of the city of Sarnia which, I hope, will serve as an example on other occasions. As hon. members are aware, the reserve is in and about Sarnia and the population is closely mixed and allied with the people of that community. We found that the school we had there was somewhat old and required repairs and we
See appendix at pages 6784-86.

negotiated an agreement with the corporation, the effect of which will be that we will pay for the construction of three classrooms as part of another school being built by the board of education of that city. We will pay a per capita annual grant to the board of education so that from now on there will be no separate Indian school in and about Sarnia and the Indian children will be free to attend not only that particular school but any of the schools in that city. I suggest that is an ideal situation and I think the plan can be worked out successfully. There may be some difficulties to overcome but I hope that will be the end of our functions with respect to education on that reserve.
I should also mention, Mr. Chairman, a very useful committee which was formed in the Ontario legislature and which visited Indians in this province throughout the past 12 months. The province was naturally concerned with the condition of those early settlers in Ontario and wished to learn for their own purposes about the economic conditions, educational standards, health standards and the like. The present government asked the legislature to appoint a committee and that was done. They toured the province in a manner which I have not found possible yet since I took over this office. I believe they visited every reserve and interviewed large numbers of chiefs and principal men. They have reported on those aspects of Indian life, not only within their own competence but within the competence of this government and, I might say, at our request and at their own desire.
We supplied them with our own good offices in every place and made whatever arrangements we could to be of assistance to them. 1 am grateful to them for the commendation they gave this department and its officials in their report for their attendance upon them and the good work which is being done in many reserves. The report suggests, without in any way transgressing on the separate fields of provincial and dominion activity, that it would be useful if we would meet with them to consider the welfare of our Indian people since, after all, it is agreed they are part of our community and every effort should be made by every level of government to assist in that work. While I have not been able to follow up that suggestion as yet, I propose to approach the provincial government having in mind the suggestion in their report and to have the officials of this department confer with them on the questions they have raised.
The citizenship branch has little to do except the registration of naturalization and
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration the maintaining of records. But as I have indicated on other occasions in the house, their work is increasing and will increase noticeably during the next two or three years. The first substantial numbers of those who came to our shores since the war came in 1947, so that a considerable number of them are now here more than the required five years and are, according to the statistics, beginning to apply for citizenship. speechtext:
Summary of the proceedings of a conference with representative Indians held in
Ottawa October 26-28, 1953.
(1)	On February 28, March 1, 2 and 3, 1951, a conference was held with representative Indians and officers of Indian associations from all those regions of Canada where there is an Indian population except the Northwest Territories. The purpose of that conference was to discuss the provisions of Bill 79 to revise the Indian Act, and a summary of the proceedings of that conference appears as appendix B, House of Commons debates, March 16, 1951.
(2)	On October 26, 27 and 28, 1953, a second conference was held in Ottawa with representative Indians and officers of Indian associations, whose names are set out in schedule "A" hereto. In addition to the representatives, the minister, deputy minister and headquarters officials of the Indian affairs branch, the conference was attended by the Indian commissioner for British Columbia and all regional supervisors from the provinces.
(3)	As in 1951, the purpose of this second conference was to discuss the provisions of the Indian Act and as well to suggest amendments to it in the light of experience gained since it came into force September 4, 1951. Much of the discussion was devoted to the administration of the act rather than specific amendments to it. Officials of the Indian affairs branch reported on particular sections of the act which they administer. Following this all sections of the act were considered.
(4)	Upon the conclusion of this phase of the work of the conference there was a general discussion on matters pertaining to the health of the Indian people with officials of the Department of National Health and Welfare.
(5)	It was again evident from the discussion that the problems of Indian communities varied from reserve to reserve and region to region and these differences accounted for the variety of viewpoints expressed towards particular sections of the act. It was the unanimous view of those present, however, that the present act had been beneficial to all Indians.
(6)	As in 1951, all of the representatives were opposed to section 86, which deals with taxation, and also section 112, which provides
for the enfranchisement of bands or individual members thereof after committees of inquiry.
(7)	With respect to section 86, all of the
representatives favoured the exemption contained in subsection (1), but thought that it did not go far enough. It was again asserted that under article, 13 of the terms of union between Canada and the province of British Columbia the Indians of British Columbia were not liable to taxation. Representations were made that the Indians in British Columbia living on reserves on the coast and conducting fishing as their only occupation are denied the benefit of tax exemption although Indians in the interior of the province and elsewhere engaged in grazing cattle on reserves enjoy that exemption. A strong argument was made that the tax exemption should be extended to Indian fishermen whether the owner of a ship or engaged in a joint venture. With respect to subsection (2), which relates to a waiver of exemption from taxation under the Canada Elections Act, it was suggested that consideration be given to allowing the Indians to vote without the necessity of executing a waiver. Two representatives, however, were opposed to forcing the right to vote on the Indians.	*
(8)	With respect to section 9, which provides for the protest of the inclusion, omission, addition or deletion of persons on band lists, three different opinions were expressed. Three representatives said that all persons who were registered on band lists at the time the act came into force should continue to be members and favoured the elimination of this section from the act, and the dropping of all protests. Eleven representatives, however, favoured the section but were of opinion that the time limit for protesting the inclusion of persons on a list should be extended beyond the six-month period provided in this section to give a further opportunity for lodging protests. One representative was in favour of section 9 as it now stands.
(9)	As in 1951 the same three views were again expressed with regard to sections 93-96

dealing with the sale and possession of intoxicants: (1) complete prohibition; (2) retention of the sections in the present act; (3) that provincial liquor laws be made applicable to Indians. Eleven representatives were of opinion that the liquor provisions in the Indian Act should be deleted and that the Indians should become subject to the provincial laws with respect to the sale and possession of intoxicants. Six representatives were in favour of retaining the present sections of the act. Two of these, however, were opposed to any extension of liquor privileges to Indians as provided by section 95 without the Indians being consulted first.
(10)	It was generally felt that the principle of registering illegitimate children set out in section 11 (e) ought to be retained. It was suggested, however, by two representatives, that illegitimate children in certain circumstances should not be allowed to benefit from the funds of the band.
(11)	Although unanimously accepted in principle in 1951, payment of a per capita share of the capital and revenue moneys of a band to persons who become voluntarily enfranchised as provided by section 15 (a) was now objected to by one representative. It was asserted that a woman member of a band could apply for enfranchisement and receive her per capita share and subsequently remarry into the band and be again enfranchised with her husband and obtain still another per capita share. It was stated that the funds of the band should remain intact for the benefit of future generations. The opposite view was taken by other representatives who were of opinion that a member of a band had an inalienable interest in the property of the band and should be entitled to take his per capita share of the moneys when leaving the band. One representative suggested that an Indian woman who marries a non-Indian should have an option of taking a per capita share of the moneys of the band or continue to share in the distribution of annuities, interest moneys and rents as provided in the former act.
(12)	Section 19, which deals with surveys and subdivisions, was opposed by the same representatives as in 1951. They contended that there are certain areas in Alberta and Saskatchewan where the subdivision of reserves is not suitable nor acceptable, and for that reason surveys and subdivisions should only be carried out with the consent of the council of the band or of the band. It was the general feeling of the other representatives that surveys were beneficial and necessary and that this work should be carried out expeditiously.
83276-429J
Conference on Indian Act
(13)	With respect to section 20 there was now no feeling that temporary possession of land led to insecurity as was the case in 1951. On the contrary, it was the feeling of several representatives that the period of temporary possession should be extended from two to five years, and possibly ten years, to find out if the Indian is capable of making proper use of the land. Seven representatives were of opinion that the present two-year period is satisfactory, while six representatives thought that the land should be granted on a temporary basis of five years or more instead of the present two years. It was also suggested by one representative that there should be some provision in the act which would permit cancellation of a certificate of possession in cases where the Indian to whom the land is allotted does not make proper use of it.
(14)	It was recommended by one representative that the provisions of section 39 should be changed to permit a surrender to be assented to by referendum with polls established at convenient places on the reserve.	.
(15)	With respect to section 60, which provides that at the request of a band the governor in council may grant to the band the right to exercise control and management over lands in the reserve as may be deemed advisable, it was suggested by one representative that this provision be amended to provide that the request be made by the council of the band rather than the band. It was mentioned that in the case of a large band it was extremely difficult to get a majority of the voters together to hold a vote to request application of this provision. It was pointed out that at the conference in 1951 when this provision was discussed, it was the general feeling of the representatives that the request should be made by the band, and this view was held this year by all the other representatives.
(16)	With regard to the voting age of band members in band elections set out in section 76, it was the opinion of seven representatives that the age should be the same as that which applies in provincial elections. However, seven other representatives were of opinion that the age should remain at twenty-one as provided in the act.
(17)	Similarly there was a difference of opinion regarding the term of office of chiefs and councillors. It was again felt by a number of representatives that the two-year term of office provided in section 77 was not sufficiently long to enable members of band councils to gain sufficient experience for the
6786	HOUSE OF
Conference on Indian Act most effective management of band affairs. A term of office of three, four and five years was suggested. On the other hand, some representatives felt that the term of office of band councils should be similar to that in effect in municipalities and the two-year term should be retained.
(18)	Section 88 was discussed at some
length but there was no opinion in favour of a change and I was asked, and gave the assurance, that there was no present intention to alter it.	.
(19)	It was suggested by one representative that a peace officer should have a warrant rather than the authority now provided in section 101.
(20)	With respect to section 108, which provides for the voluntary enfranchisement of Indians, one representative objected to the minor unmarried children being enfranchised with their parents. It was considered by this representative that such children should be given the option at age twenty-one of being enfranchised or retaining membership in the band. It was also suggested by this representative that an Indian woman who marries a non-Indian and is subsequently deserted or widowed should be able to return to band membership with the consent of the band council or the band, and that minor unmarried children of an Indian woman who marries a non-Indian should not be automatically enfranchised. Another representative objected to the automatic enfranchisement of an Indian woman who marries a nonIndian because such woman would be deprived of any right to an interest in subsequent sales of land which was given the members of the Indian band and their posterity forever.
(21)	Section 110(2), (3) and (4), which provides for the grant of land to enfranchised Indians was unanimously approved by the representatives in 1951, but was objected to this year by one representative who considered that these provisions should be deleted from the act. This objection was not based on experience as there have been no decisions made under these provisions.
(22)	With respect to section 120, it was recommended by one representative that all schools should be non-denominational except the minimum number of residential schools required to take care of unfortunate children. However, arrangements should be made for religious instruction in such schools by a clergyman of the appropriate faith. Another
